title: Earth's four spheres
description: Scientists describe Earth as four overlapping spheres: rock (geosphere), air (atmosphere), water in every form (hydrosphere) and life (biosphere).

facts.text: Scientists describe Earth in spheres: the solid, rocky Earth (the lithosphere or geosphere), the atmosphere of air above it, the hydrosphere of water, and the biosphere, the parts of Earth where life exists, which overlaps all the others.
The hydrosphere is all of a planet's water, on the surface, underground and in the air, whether it is liquid, vapor or ice.

title: The spheres are linked
description: Earth's spheres trade water, gas and energy: plants move soil water into the air, and big eruptions put sulfur into the sky that cools the planet.

facts.text: In transpiration, roots take up water from the soil and leaves release it into the air as water vapor through tiny pores (stomata); a large oak tree can transpire about 40,000 gallons (151,000 liters) a year.

After big explosive eruptions, ash falls out of the stratosphere within days to weeks, but sulfur dioxide turns into sulfuric acid droplets that reflect sunlight; several eruptions in the past century cooled Earth's surface for one to three years.

title: What makes a mineral
description: A mineral is a natural solid with a set chemical recipe and an orderly arrangement of atoms, usually formed without living things. Ice qualifies; liquid water does not.

facts.text: A mineral is a naturally occurring, homogeneous solid with a definite chemical composition and a highly ordered atomic arrangement, usually formed by inorganic processes.
Ice, the solid form of water, qualifies as a mineral; liquid water does not.
Quartz is silica, silicon dioxide (SiO2), and its varieties include purple amethyst, yellow citrine, pink rose quartz and smoky quartz.

title: Rocks are made of minerals
description: A rock is a mix of one or more minerals. Scientists recognize just over 6,000 minerals, and common rocks like granite and sandstone are built from a few of them.

facts.text: A rock is an aggregate of one or more minerals; common rocks include granite, basalt, limestone and sandstone, and common minerals include quartz, feldspar, mica and calcite.
The International Mineralogical Association recognizes just over 6,000 mineral species, and in recent years it has accepted more than a hundred new species a year.

title: The Mohs hardness scale
description: Mohs ranked ten minerals from talc (1) to diamond (10): a harder mineral scratches a softer one. The scale gives an order, not equal steps.

facts.text: The Mohs scale, devised in 1812 by German mineralogist Friedrich Mohs, ranks ten minerals by scratch hardness: talc (1), gypsum, calcite, fluorite, apatite, orthoclase, quartz (7), topaz, corundum and diamond (10); a harder mineral scratches a softer one.
On the Mohs scale a fingernail rates about 2.2, a copper penny about 3.2, a pocketknife about 5.1 and a glass plate about 5.5.
The Mohs scale is not linear: going from calcite (3) to fluorite (4) is roughly a 25% increase in hardness, while going from corundum (9) to diamond (10) is more than 300%.

title: Streak and luster
description: A mineral's streak (the color of its powder) is more reliable than its color, and its luster (how it reflects light) narrows the choices further.

facts.text: A mineral's streak is the color of its powder, made by scraping it across unglazed porcelain (a streak plate); the streak is usually more consistent than the mineral's apparent color, which can vary a lot.
Hematite ranges from red and brown to black, gray and silver, yet it always leaves a reddish streak; its name comes from the Greek word for blood.
Pyrite, nicknamed fool's gold for its gold color and metallic luster, leaves a greenish-black streak, while real gold leaves a yellow streak.
Luster describes how a mineral reflects light; a metallic luster looks like metal and belongs to opaque minerals such as pyrite and galena, while quartz usually has a vitreous (glassy) luster.

title: The crust's most common minerals
description: Silicate minerals, built on oxygen and silicon, make up most of the crust. Feldspars alone are more than half of it, and quartz comes second.

facts.text: Silicon and oxygen are the two most abundant elements in Earth's crust, and silicate minerals make up about 95% of Earth's crust and upper mantle.
Feldspars make up more than half of Earth's crust.
Quartz is the second most abundant mineral in Earth's crust after feldspar; it rates 7 on the Mohs scale and is highly resistant to weathering, so it concentrates in sandstones.

title: What granite is made of
description: Granite is mostly feldspar and quartz, often with flakes of mica, a mineral that splits into thin, elastic sheets.

facts.text: Granite's main minerals are feldspars and quartz, often with mica (muscovite or biotite); in some granites the feldspar is reddish orange and the quartz nearly white.
Mica's defining property is perfect cleavage into thin elastic sheets; biotite mica is black, brown or dark greenish brown.

title: Why sand is mostly quartz
description: Quartz is common, hard, has almost no cleavage and barely dissolves or decomposes, so it outlasts other minerals and ends up as most of the world's sand.

facts.text: Quartz is by far the commonest mineral in sand because it is abundant in rocks, comparatively hard, has practically no cleavage, is nearly insoluble in water and does not decompose.

title: Cooling rate and crystal size
description: Magma that cools slowly underground grows big crystals (intrusive rock); lava chilled fast at the surface makes tiny crystals (extrusive rock), or glass like obsidian.

facts.text: Intrusive (plutonic) igneous rocks cool slowly deep in the crust, growing crystals big enough to see without magnification; extrusive (volcanic) rocks cool rapidly at the surface, giving microscopic crystals or glass.
Slow cooling deep underground gives ions time to migrate and build large crystals, while magma erupted at the surface is chilled so quickly that its minerals have little or no chance to grow.
Obsidian is a natural volcanic glass formed when viscous lava cools so rapidly that it solidifies before crystals can grow.

title: Granite versus basalt
description: Granite is coarse, light and intrusive, the typical rock of continents; basalt is fine-grained, dark, iron- and magnesium-rich and extrusive, the main rock of the ocean floor.

facts.text: Granite is a coarse- to medium-grained intrusive igneous rock that cools slowly at depth and is the most common plutonic rock of Earth's crust; continental crust is mostly granites.
Basalt is an extrusive igneous rock, usually very fine-grained, dark and comparatively rich in iron and magnesium; oceanic crust is mostly basalts.
As a lava flow cools it contracts and cracks into columns, most of them six-sided; Devils Postpile in California is a famous example.

title: From sediment to rock
description: Loose sediment becomes sedimentary rock when layers are compacted and minerals cement the grains together. Such rocks cover most land but are a thin skin on the crust.

facts.text: Sedimentary rocks make up about 75% of Earth's exposed land surface but only about 5% of Earth's crust by volume.
Loose sediment becomes sedimentary rock through compaction under pressure and cementation, as minerals precipitate in the pore spaces between grains.

title: Sandstone, shale and limestone
description: Sandstone started as sand, shale as mud, and limestone largely as the shells of sea creatures. Shale is by far the most common.

facts.text: Sandstone is made of sand-sized grains, 0.063 to 2 mm across, mostly quartz, held together by a cement such as silica or calcium carbonate.
Shale is a fine-grained sedimentary rock of silt- and clay-sized particles that splits into thin layers; it is the most abundant sedimentary rock, roughly 70% of the total.
Limestone is mostly calcium carbonate, usually as calcite, and in many limestones the grains are microscopic fragments of fossil shells from lime-secreting sea life.

title: Metamorphic rock: changed, not melted
description: Heat, pressure and hot fluids transform existing rock without melting it. Limestone recrystallizes into marble, whose round calcite grains never line up in layers.

facts.text: Metamorphic rocks form when igneous, sedimentary or older metamorphic rocks are changed by high heat, high pressure or hot mineral-rich fluids; the rock does not melt but becomes denser and more compact as its minerals rearrange or react.
Marble is limestone or dolomite that has recrystallized under heat, pressure and fluids; its main mineral is calcite.
The marble for Michelangelo's David came from the Carrara quarries in Tuscany; he began carving on September 13, 1501, and finished in 1504.

title: Foliation: shale into slate
description: Pressure lines up flat minerals into parallel sheets (foliation). That turns shale into slate, which splits into thin slabs; schist and gneiss are foliated too.

facts.text: Foliation forms when pressure squeezes flat or elongate minerals in a rock so they line up; minerals that are not flat, such as those in limestone, cannot align, and rocks like gneiss and schist are strongly banded or foliated.
Slate is a fine-grained metamorphic rock formed from mudstone or shale; pressure gives it cleavage, so it splits into thin slabs used for roofing, flooring and blackboards.

title: What makes a gem
description: Gems are prized for beauty, durability and rarity. Ruby and sapphire are the same mineral, corundum, colored by different trace elements.

facts.text: Gemstones are minerals highly prized for beauty (from color, clarity, luster and optical effects), durability and rarity; durability means a stone keeps its polish and withstands constant handling, and some non-mineral materials such as pearl, coral and amber are also gemstones.

Corundum is aluminum oxide, rated 9 on the Mohs scale and second in hardness only to diamond; pure corundum is colorless, ruby is red corundum colored by chromium, and sapphire's blue comes from iron and titanium.

title: What makes an ore
description: An ore is rock with minerals that can be mined and sold at a profit: an economic label, not a geological one. Hematite is a key iron ore.

facts.text: An ore is a natural aggregation of minerals that can be mined and sold for profit; hematite and magnetite are ore minerals of iron, and chalcopyrite of copper.

'Ore deposit' is an economic term and 'mineral deposit' a geological one: every ore deposit is a mineral deposit but not the reverse, and whether a deposit pays depends on its concentration, size, mining and transport costs and market prices.

title: What soil is made of
description: Healthy soil is about half solids (mostly mineral bits sorted into sand, silt and clay, plus organic matter) and half pore space holding water and air. Five factors shape it.

facts.text: A typical soil in good condition is about 45% mineral matter, 25% air, 25% water and 5% organic matter; the mineral matter is tiny rock fragments classed by size as sand, silt and clay, and clay particles need a powerful microscope to see.
Soils are complex mixtures of minerals, water, air, organic matter and countless organisms, with organic matter being the decaying remains of once-living things.

A soil develops as its parent material weathers, shaped by five factors: parent material, climate, living organisms, topography and time; where all five are the same the soil is the same, and where any differs the soils differ.

title: Soil horizons
description: Dig a soil pit and you see layers: O (organic), A (topsoil), E (leached), B (subsoil), C (parent material) and R (bedrock, which is not soil).

facts.text: A soil profile is made of horizons: O (mostly organic matter such as decomposing leaves), A (topsoil, minerals mixed with organic matter), E (leached, missing in some soils), B (subsoil, where leached minerals accumulate) and C (parent material).
Under the C horizon lies R, bedrock such as granite, basalt, quartzite, limestone or sandstone; bedrock is not soil.

title: Quartzite: sandstone remade
description: Heat and pressure recrystallize quartz sandstone into quartzite, so tough that it breaks through its grains and resists weathering.

facts.text: Quartzite is sandstone converted into solid quartz rock, including by recrystallization under heat and pressure; it breaks through, not around, its sand grains, leaving a smooth surface, and it is extremely resistant to weathering, so it often stands up as hills.

title: Where Earth's inner heat comes from
description: Earth's interior is heated by heat left over from its formation, by radioactive decay (about half) and by the core slowly freezing.

facts.text: Earth's internal heat comes from the decay of radioactive elements, heat left over from the planet's formation, and heat released as the liquid outer core solidifies onto the inner core.

In 2011 the KamLAND detector, a tank of about 1,000 tonnes of mineral oil deep underground in Japan, caught geoneutrinos from uranium and thorium decay and showed that radioactive decay supplies about half of Earth's heat; the rest is likely mostly heat left over from Earth's formation.
In most places, rock gets hotter with depth by about 25 degrees Celsius for every kilometer you go down (the geothermal gradient).

title: Convection carries the heat out
description: Mantle rock heated from below rises slowly while cooler, denser rock sinks; this convection carries heat outward and drives the plates.

facts.text: Mantle convection carries heat from the core toward the lithosphere: mantle rock rises as it heats and sinks as it cools, delivering hot material to plate boundaries and hotspots and carrying cooler material back down through subduction.

title: What each boundary does to the crust
description: At divergent boundaries plates move apart and new crust forms; at transform boundaries plates slide past each other and crust is neither made nor destroyed.

facts.text: At divergent boundaries, plates move apart and new crust is created by magma pushing up from the mantle.
At Thingvellir in Iceland, the North American and Eurasian plates break apart and the land between them subsides into a rift; the spreading averages about 2 cm a year.
At transform boundaries, plates slide horizontally past each other and crust is neither produced nor destroyed; California's San Andreas Fault zone is one.

title: Three kinds of collision
description: Convergent boundaries come in three kinds: ocean under continent (the Andes), ocean under ocean (island arcs like the Marianas) and continent against continent (the Himalayas).

facts.text: Where an ocean plate meets a continent, the ocean plate is subducted beneath it; the Nazca Plate diving under South America built the Andes, and this kind of boundary feeds volcanoes such as those of the Andes and the Cascades.

Where two ocean plates converge, one is subducted under the other, forming a deep trench and a curved chain of volcanic islands; the Mariana Trench and Islands mark where the Pacific Plate dives beneath the Philippine Plate.
When two continents collide, neither is easily subducted and the crust crumples upward; India's collision with Asia about 50 million years ago built the Himalayas.

title: How hotspots leave chains
description: A plate moving over a mostly stationary hotspot carries each volcano away, leaving a chain that gets older in the direction the plate moves.

facts.text: In 1963 the Canadian geophysicist J. Tuzo Wilson proposed that the Hawaiian-Emperor chain formed as the Pacific Plate moved over a deep, stationary hotspot, with volcanoes growing over it and dying as they were carried away.
Each island or submerged seamount in the Hawaiian chain is successively older toward the northwest, recording the Pacific Plate's motion over the hotspot.

The Hawaiian-Emperor chain has a 60 degree bend, dated to about 47 million years ago, between the younger Hawaiian chain and the older Emperor chain; a 2017 study concluded that explaining it takes both a change in the Pacific Plate's direction and movement of the hotspot itself.

title: Yellowstone: a hotspot under a continent
description: The North American Plate moving southwest over the Yellowstone hotspot left a trail of volcanic fields across southern Idaho that gets older to the southwest.

facts.text: The Yellowstone hotspot's trail of volcanic rocks begins about 17 million years ago in northern Nevada and southern Oregon and gets younger across southern Idaho to Yellowstone National Park.

The North American Plate has been moving west-southwest over the Yellowstone hotspot, leaving a chain of volcanic centers across the Snake River Plain; Yellowstone's geysers and hot springs are the hotspot's current expression.

title: Normal, reverse and strike-slip faults
description: Faults are named by how the blocks move: the hanging wall drops (normal), rides up (reverse or thrust), or the blocks slide sideways (strike-slip).

facts.text: A fault is a fracture or zone of fractures between two blocks of rock, along which the blocks move relative to each other.
On a tilted fault, the block of rock above the fault is the hanging wall and the block below it is the footwall.
On a strike-slip fault, the two blocks slide horizontally past one another; the San Andreas Fault is a right-lateral strike-slip fault.
A thrust fault is a reverse fault that dips less than 45 degrees; reverse and thrust faults are common in mountain ranges and where plates converge.

title: Faults record stretching or squeezing
description: Normal faults form where the crust is stretched (extension), reverse faults where it is squeezed (compression).

facts.text: On a normal fault, the hanging wall moves down relative to the footwall; normal faulting happens where the crust is stretched (extension).
On a reverse fault, the hanging wall moves up and over the footwall; reverse faulting is common where the crust is squeezed (compression).
The Basin and Range Province of the western United States is an extensive network of horsts and grabens: blocks left high as ranges and blocks dropped down as basins between normal faults.

title: P, S and surface waves
description: P waves push and pull and arrive first; S waves shear side to side and cannot cross liquids; surface waves arrive last; S and surface waves do the damage.

facts.text: P waves are compressional waves that squeeze and stretch the ground in the direction they travel; at 5 or 6 km per second they are the fastest seismic waves, and they can move through solids and liquids.
S waves are shear waves that move the ground perpendicular to their direction of travel, at about 3 km per second, slower than P waves, and they cannot pass through liquids.
Surface waves travel more slowly than P and S waves but can have very large amplitudes; Rayleigh waves make a long rolling motion and Love waves shake the ground side to side.
P waves are the first to shake a building, but the S waves and surface waves that follow do the damage, because buildings are more easily damaged by horizontal motion than by vertical motion.

title: Early warning uses the P-wave head start
description: ShakeAlert detects the fast P waves and sends alerts ahead of the slower, damaging waves; it warns of a quake already under way and does not predict one.

facts.text: P waves travel almost twice as fast as the damaging S waves and surface waves, so ShakeAlert, the USGS earthquake early warning system for California, Oregon and Washington, detects them and sends alerts that can arrive before strong shaking.
Earthquake early warning is not earthquake prediction: it detects an earthquake that has already begun and alerts people before the shaking reaches them.

title: The San Andreas: locked and creeping
description: The San Andreas is the Pacific-North American transform boundary; locked sections produce great quakes, while a central creeping section slips steadily with only small ones.

facts.text: The San Andreas Fault zone runs about 1,300 km through California, where the Pacific Plate grinds northwest past the North American Plate.

Locked sections of the San Andreas produced the M 7.9 Fort Tejon earthquake of 1857 and the M 7.9 San Francisco earthquake of 1906, while the creeping section between San Juan Bautista and Parkfield produces many small earthquakes (mostly M 5 and smaller) but no large ones.
The San Francisco earthquake struck at 5:12 a.m. on April 18, 1906, and ruptured more than 400 km of the San Andreas Fault (USGS gives 477 km, 296 miles).

title: Elastic rebound
description: While a fault is locked, moving plates bend the rock beside it and store strain; when the fault slips, the rock snaps back, and that is the earthquake.

facts.text: Studying how the ground moved in 1906, Henry Fielding Reid concluded that earthquakes are an 'elastic rebound': the crust gradually stores elastic strain as the plates move, bending features like fences into an S shape, then releases it suddenly.
In the 1906 earthquake, a fence crossing the San Andreas Fault was offset about 8.5 feet (about 2.6 m).

title: Magnitude versus intensity
description: A quake has one magnitude but many intensities: shaking depends on distance from the rupture, depth and the ground underfoot (bedrock least, soft mud most).

facts.text: An earthquake has a single magnitude, but its shaking (intensity) varies from place to place, depending mostly on distance from the fault rupture; in the US, intensity is rated on the Modified Mercalli scale in Roman numerals.

The shallower M 6.7 Northridge, California, earthquake (3 to 11 miles deep) shook harder and over a wider area than the slightly larger but deeper M 6.8 Nisqually, Washington, earthquake (30 to 36 miles deep).
The type of ground changes shaking: bedrock shakes the least, and soft mud the most.

title: Liquefaction
description: Strong shaking can make loose, waterlogged sediment lose its strength and act like a liquid, as it did under San Francisco's Marina District in 1989.

facts.text: Liquefaction happens when loose, water-logged sediments near the surface lose their strength in strong shaking, much as wet sand gives way when you wiggle your toes at the beach; sand and water can bubble up as sand boils.
In the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake, liquefied soils beneath San Francisco's Marina district caused major sinking, fracturing and horizontal sliding of the ground.

The 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake (moment magnitude 6.9) had its epicenter near Loma Prieta peak, south of San Francisco; the city's Marina district was particularly hard hit because it was built on filled land of loose, sandy soil.

title: Runny and sticky magma
description: Silica makes magma viscous; gas escapes easily from runny low-silica basalt, which erupts quietly, but is trapped in sticky high-silica magma, which tends to explode.

facts.text: Viscosity is a lava's resistance to flow; more silica makes longer, more tangled molecular chains, like spaghetti, so low-silica basalt is runny and erupts quietly while high-silica magma is sticky and likely to erupt explosively.
Gas escapes more easily from thin, runny magma than from thick, sticky magma, as you can see in the spattering of bubbling jam.

title: Shield, cinder cone and stratovolcano
description: Fluid basalt flows build broad shields like Mauna Loa; cinders build cones like Paricutin; alternating lava and ash build steep stratovolcanoes like Fuji and St. Helens.

facts.text: Shield volcanoes are built of thousands of fluid basalt lava flows into broad, gently sloping domes; Hawaii's Mauna Loa is the largest active volcano on Earth.

Composite volcanoes, or stratovolcanoes, are steep, symmetrical cones built of alternating layers of lava flows, ash and cinders; examples include Mount Fuji in Japan and Mount St. Helens in Washington.
Paricutin, a cinder cone, began growing on a farm in Mexico in 1943 and erupted for nine years.

title: What an eruption releases
description: Eruptions release lava (slow, rarely deadly, but destructive), ash (hard, jagged rock and glass) and gas (mostly water vapor, plus carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide).

facts.text: Most lava flows move slowly enough that people can get out of the way, so they rarely kill directly, but they knock over, bury or burn what lies in their path and can bury land under tens of meters of rock.
Volcanic ash is small, jagged pieces of rock, minerals and volcanic glass less than 2 mm across; unlike soft ash from burning wood, it is hard and abrasive, and wind can carry it thousands of miles.
By far the most abundant volcanic gas is water vapor, which is harmless; volcanoes also emit carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide.

title: Pyroclastic flows
description: A pyroclastic flow is a fast, scorching avalanche of rock, ash and gas; too fast to escape, it is the deadliest volcanic hazard.

facts.text: Pyroclastic flows are hot mixes of lava blocks, pumice, ash and gas that race across the ground typically faster than 80 km per hour, at 200 to 700 degrees Celsius, knocking down, burying or carrying away nearly everything in their path.
Pyroclastic flows are considered the most deadly of all volcano hazards.
On May 8, 1902, a pyroclastic flow (a nuee ardente, or glowing cloud) from Mount Pelee destroyed the port town of Saint-Pierre on Martinique.

title: Reading hazards from the plate setting
description: Subduction zones produce the largest earthquakes and explosive, silica-rich volcanoes; other settings bring their own quakes and eruptions.

facts.text: The world's largest earthquakes, magnitude 9 and above, occur in subduction zones, where one plate slides beneath another.
The Cascade volcanoes, from southern British Columbia to northern California, sit above a subduction zone; their high-silica magma is thick and pasty and traps gas, so they can erupt explosively.

title: Mechanical weathering: ice and roots
description: Weathering breaks rock down where it sits. Freezing water expands and wedges cracks apart, most of all where temperatures swing across freezing; roots pry cracks open as they grow.

facts.text: Weathering is the breakdown of rock in place, at or near Earth's surface; it is often divided into mechanical weathering, which breaks rock apart, and chemical weathering, which changes its minerals, while erosion transports the broken pieces away.
When water freezes into ice it expands by about 9%, so water freezing in a crack acts as a wedge that pushes the rock apart.
Frost wedging is most effective where temperatures swing between freezing and thawing again and again.
Plant roots work their way into cracks in rock and pry it apart as they grow.

title: Chemical weathering: carbonic acid and clay
description: Carbon dioxide dissolves in rain and soil water to make weak carbonic acid, which turns feldspar into clay and rusts iron minerals, while quartz is virtually unaffected.

facts.text: Carbon dioxide dissolves in water to make a weak acid, carbonic acid, that can dissolve rock; biological processes make soil much richer in carbon dioxide than the air, so water seeping through soil becomes more acidic.
Carbonic acid reacts with feldspars to form clay minerals, while quartz is very resistant to chemical weathering.
Oxidation rusts iron-bearing minerals, and oxidized basalt turns reddish instead of dark gray or black.

title: How limestone caves form
description: Water made acidic by carbon dioxide, mostly in the soil, seeps into cracks in limestone and dissolves it into caves; caves, sinking streams and sinkholes form karst.

facts.text: Solution caves form when water made acidic by carbon dioxide, picked up mostly in the soil, seeps down through cracks and weak spots in limestone and dissolves it.
Caves, sinking streams and sinkholes together form karst, a landscape made in limestone and other rocks that dissolve.
Mammoth Cave in Kentucky, formed as water dissolved limestone, is the longest known cave system in the world, with at least 400 miles (650 km) of mapped passages.

title: How stalactites and stalagmites grow
description: Dripping water loses carbon dioxide and leaves calcite behind, building stalactites down from the ceiling and stalagmites up from the floor.

facts.text: Stalactites hang from cave ceilings and stalagmites rise from the floor; both are built mostly of calcite left behind as dripping water loses carbon dioxide, and the two can join into a column.
The simplest stalactite is a thin, hollow stone tube called a soda straw.

title: How sinkholes form
description: Sinkholes form where groundwater dissolves limestone, salt or gypsum underground; some settle gradually, others collapse abruptly when a cavity roof fails.

facts.text: Sinkholes form where groundwater dissolves limestone, salt, gypsum or other soluble rock underground; some settle gradually, while cover-collapse sinkholes can open abruptly, over hours, when the roof over a cavity collapses.

title: How a river carries its load
description: A river moves bed load along its bottom, suspended load in the water and dissolved load in solution; faster water moves bigger particles, and slowing water drops them.

facts.text: A river carries large particles as bed load, pushed or bounced (saltation) along the bottom; smaller particles held up in the water as suspended load; and a dissolved load of ions such as calcium, on average about 15% of the mass it carries.
How fast water flows controls which particle sizes it can erode and carry, and when a stream slows, the sediment it can no longer carry settles out.

title: Why river valleys are V-shaped
description: A river erodes mainly downward along its bed, so river-cut valleys have a V-shaped cross-section; glaciers widen them into U shapes.

facts.text: A stream erodes mainly downward along its bed, so a stream-carved valley has a V-shaped cross-section; glaciers, wider and eroding both their base and sides, turn such valleys into U shapes.

title: How meanders move and leave oxbow lakes
description: On a bend, fast water erodes the outer bank while sediment builds up on the inner bank; when the river cuts through a loop, the old channel becomes an oxbow lake.

facts.text: On a river bend, water flows fastest on the outside, wearing away the outer bank, and slowest on the inside, where silt and sediment build up.
When a river cuts through the narrow neck of a meander to shorten its course, the abandoned loop becomes an oxbow lake, named for the U-shaped collar on an ox's neck.

title: How floods build floodplains and levees
description: Floodwater spreading over the floodplain slows and drops coarse sediment by the channel as natural levees and fine silt farther out, making floodplains fertile.

facts.text: When a flooding river overtops its banks and spreads over its floodplain, the water slows sharply and drops its coarser sediment near the channel, building natural levees, while finer silt and clay settle across the floodplain.

A floodplain is the generally flat land beside a river; floods spread nutrient-rich silt across it, making floodplains very fertile farmland, and ancient Egyptian culture grew up on the Nile's floodplain.

title: How deltas grow and shrink
description: A river slows at its mouth and drops its sediment, building a delta crossed by distributaries; cut off the sediment supply and the delta shrinks, as on the Nile.

facts.text: A river slows as it reaches its mouth, so its sediment falls to the bottom and builds a delta, crossed by smaller branching channels called distributaries.
The word delta comes from the triangle-shaped Greek capital letter delta (Δ), the shape of the Nile's delta; the Mississippi instead builds a bird's-foot delta.
The Nile delta is shrinking because the Aswan High Dam and other river management hold back the sediment that once reached it, so the coast erodes.

title: How glaciers erode
description: Glaciers pluck blocks from bedrock and abrade it with the rocks they carry, leaving striations, and scour floor and walls into U-shaped valleys.

facts.text: Glaciers erode by plucking, in which ice freezes onto bedrock and pulls pieces away, and by abrasion, in which rocks embedded in the base of the ice grind the bedrock, leaving polish and long grooves called striations.
Valley glaciers erode the whole valley, widening its floor and over-steepening its walls, and leave a flat-bottomed, steep-walled U-shaped valley.

title: Glacial landforms: cirques, horns and fjords
description: Glaciers carve bowl-shaped cirques; three or more cirques eating into a peak leave arêtes and a horn such as the Matterhorn; fjords are glacial valleys the sea flooded after the ice melted.

facts.text: Cirques are bowl-shaped hollows that glaciers carve high on mountains, where most mountain glaciers form; lakes called tarns often fill them after the ice retreats.

When three or more cirques erode into a mountain from different sides, they leave knife-edged ridges called arêtes and a sharp peak called a horn; the Matterhorn in the Swiss Alps is a famous example.
A fjord is a long, narrow arm of the sea filling a glacier-carved valley whose floor lies below sea level; after the glaciers melted, the sea flooded in.
Norway's Sognefjord is 1,308 m deep.

title: How wind erodes deserts
description: Wind removes fine particles (deflation), leaving desert pavement, and sandblasts rock into ventifacts and yardangs; only about 20% of deserts are sand.

facts.text: Sand covers only about 20% of Earth's deserts, while nearly half of desert surfaces are plains where the wind has removed fine material and exposed loose gravel.
Deflation is the wind's removal of loose, fine particles, and it often leaves desert pavement, a sheetlike surface of rock fragments.
Windblown sand cuts and sometimes polishes rocks into flat faces, making ventifacts, and desert winds streamline ridges called yardangs, up to tens of meters high and kilometers long.

title: How sand dunes move
description: Sand bounces along by saltation, climbs a dune's gentle upwind slope and avalanches down the steep slipface, so the dune moves downwind.

facts.text: Wind moves sand grains mostly by saltation: they bounce along close to the ground.
Sand grains move up a dune's gentle upwind slope; at the crest they spill down the steep slipface in tiny avalanches, so grain by grain the dune moves downwind.

title: Why slopes fail
description: A landslide happens when gravity's down-slope pull beats a slope's strength; water, undercutting, earthquakes and digging tip the balance.

facts.text: A landslide is the movement of a mass of rock, debris or earth down a slope; it happens when forces acting down-slope, mainly gravity, exceed the strength of the material, and movements are classed as falls, topples, slides, spreads and flows.

Landslides can be triggered by rainfall, snowmelt, changes in water level, stream erosion, changes in groundwater, earthquakes, volcanic activity and human disturbance, and they occur in every US state and territory.
Extra water typically weakens sandy slope material by reducing the friction between its particles, and a rising water table adds load to the slope.
Oversteepening the base of a slope, by natural erosion such as a stream cutting into it or by excavation, builds up the stresses that set off landslides.

title: Debris flows and burned slopes
description: Debris flows are fast landslides of water, mud and rock; after wildfire, burned ground absorbs less rain, so modest storms can trigger them.

facts.text: Debris flows are fast-moving landslides of water, mud, rocks and vegetation that can surge downslope like flowing concrete, often faster than a person can run and at speeds that can exceed 35 mph.
After a wildfire removes vegetation and changes the soil, the ground absorbs less rain, so even modest storms can trigger debris flows on steep burned slopes.

title: Differential erosion: hard over soft
description: Hard caprock resists erosion and shields softer rock below, leaving mesas and buttes; in the Appalachians, resistant sandstones hold up ridges while shale and limestone floor the valleys.

facts.text: Mesas and buttes are topped by hard caprock that resists weathering and erosion and protects the softer layers beneath; buttes form as streams cut through a mesa or plateau.
A mesa is a broad, flat-topped landform with at least one steep side; a butte is smaller, with steep slopes on all sides, and usually taller than it is wide.
In the Appalachians' Valley and Ridge region, resistant sandstones and conglomerates hold up the ridges, while limestones and shales, which erode more easily, make up much of the valleys.

title: How hoodoos form
description: At Bryce Canyon, caprock shields softer rock as fins, frost wedging opens windows, and when the caprock collapses, spires called hoodoos remain.

facts.text: At Bryce Canyon, harder caprock layers preserve softer rock below as rock walls called fins; ice widening cracks breaks holes called windows through them; as the windows grow, the caprock collapses, leaving spires called hoodoos.
Bryce Canyon's amphitheater holds the greatest concentration of hoodoos on Earth.
At Bryce Canyon, slightly acidic rain dissolves the calcium carbonate that cements the rock together.

title: How stone arches form
description: In Arches National Park, salt-pushed domes cracked the sandstone, erosion shaped fins, and dissolving cement and freezing water wore through the sides of fins into arches.

facts.text: Arches National Park in Utah has more than 2,000 documented arches.

In Arches National Park, buried salt pushed the rock above into domes that cracked into roughly parallel lines; erosion shaped the cracked sandstone into fins, and water dissolving the calcite cement and freezing water prying the rock apart wore through the sides of fins into arches.

title: Mountain height: uplift against erosion
description: Young ranges like the Himalayas are still being pushed up faster than they wear down; old ranges like the Appalachians have eroded for hundreds of millions of years.

facts.text: The Himalayas began rising when India collided with Asia about 40 to 50 million years ago, and they are still rising more than 1 cm a year, a rate of 10 km in a million years.
Mount Everest, the highest mountain in the world, stands about 8,849 m above sea level.

The Appalachians formed in continental collisions between about 500 and 300 million years ago and have been eroding for the past 300 million years; geologists think their peaks were once far higher, perhaps as high as today's Himalayas and Alps.
Mount Mitchell, the highest point in the Appalachians, is 2,037 m (6,684 ft) high.

title: Isostasy: mountains float and rebound
description: Mountains have light, deep roots in the denser mantle, like an iceberg; as erosion removes weight, the crust slowly rebounds upward.

facts.text: High mountains have low-density roots that extend deep into the denser mantle, like an iceberg with most of its bulk underwater; when erosion removes weight over tens of millions of years, the crust rebounds upward.

title: The Mississippi: one river, a continent's sediment
description: The Mississippi River and its tributaries drain about 40% of the continental United States, gathering sediment from 31 states toward one delta.

facts.text: The Mississippi River and its tributaries drain about 40% of the continental United States, all or parts of 31 states and two Canadian provinces.

title: Hutton: slow processes, immense time
description: James Hutton argued in 1785 that erosion, deposition and uplift repeat in slow cycles, so Earth must be immensely old, far older than the few thousand years many then assumed.

facts.text: James Hutton (1726 to 1797), a Scottish geologist, presented papers to the Royal Society of Edinburgh in 1785 arguing that erosion, deposition, sedimentation and uplift are cyclical and have repeated many times, so the age of the Earth must be inconceivably great.
In Hutton's time, a widely held view was that the Earth was only about 6,000 years old.

title: Hutton's unconformity at Siccar Point
description: At Siccar Point, Scotland, nearly vertical rock layers lie under gently sloping red sandstone. Hutton read the gap between them as a long cycle of deposition, tilting, uplift, erosion and burial.

facts.text: In June 1788 James Hutton, with John Playfair and James Hall, visited Siccar Point on the Berwickshire coast of Scotland.

At Siccar Point, nearly vertical layers of greywacke sandstone and mudstone are covered by younger, gently sloping layers of red sandstone; a surface where two sets of rock formed at different times meet is called an unconformity.

Because sediment settles in flat layers, Hutton reasoned that the vertical beds at Siccar Point had been tilted and raised above the sea, worn down by erosion, then submerged and covered by new horizontal layers.
John Playfair wrote that looking at Siccar Point made the mind giddy, looking so far into 'the abyss of time'.

title: Superposition: oldest at the bottom
description: Sediment settles in flat layers, so in an undisturbed stack the oldest layer is at the bottom and the youngest on top. It gives order, not ages in years.

facts.text: In 1669 Nicolas Steno stated that sediment settles out of water in horizontal layers (original horizontality) and that in a stack of layers the oldest is at the bottom and the youngest on top (superposition), unless later processes disturb them.
Superposition gives relative time, not age in years: two layers could have formed millions of years apart or a few hours apart.
Superposition can mislead where layers were overturned or older rock was pushed up over younger rock, as can happen when mountain belts form.

title: Cross-cutting: the cutter is younger
description: A rock body or structure that cuts across other rocks is younger than they are: a dike of cooled magma, a fault or an erosion surface comes after the rocks it cuts.

facts.text: Under the principle of cross-cutting relationships, younger rocks or structures cut across older ones: an intrusion of magma, such as a dike, is younger than the rocks it intrudes, and a fault is younger than the layers it breaks.
An erosion surface is younger than the rocks it wears away.

title: William Smith and faunal succession
description: William Smith found that fossils appear in the same order in rock layers wherever you look, which let him identify layers by their fossils and map England and Wales in 1815.

facts.text: William Smith (1769 to 1839), an English surveyor working on canals in the 1790s, observed that fossils in sedimentary rock appear in a certain order from bottom to top and that the same order is found in rocks elsewhere, the principle of faunal succession.
Using fossils to identify rock layers, William Smith published a geologic map of England and Wales in 1815.

title: Index fossils
description: Index fossils are easy to recognize, abundant, widespread and short-lived species, so rocks that hold them can be matched in age across continents.

facts.text: A useful index fossil is distinctive or easy to recognize, abundant, spread over a wide geographic area and from a species with a short range through geologic time.

Because fossils record the progressive development of life, geologists use index fossils to identify rocks of the same age throughout the world: distant rocks with the same index species formed while that species lived.
Ammonoids, extinct marine animals, are among the fossils used as index fossils.

title: Radioactive decay as a clock
description: A radioactive parent atom turns into a daughter atom at a steady rate measured by its half-life, so the amounts of parent and daughter in a rock tell how long the clock has run.

facts.text: In radioactive decay an unstable parent isotope turns into a daughter isotope of a new element; the half-life is the time it takes for half of the parent isotope in a sample to decay, and measuring parent and daughter amounts lets scientists calculate a rock's age.
Uranium-238 decays to lead-206 with a half-life of about 4.5 billion years, one of the slow clocks used to date ancient rocks.
Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5,730 years and is taken up by living things, so radiocarbon dating works only on once-living material from about the past 50,000 years.

title: Uranium-lead dating in zircon
description: Zircon takes in uranium but rejects lead as it crystallizes, so its lead comes from decay. Radiometric dates mark when a rock crystallized, so geologists date igneous rock and volcanic ash.

facts.text: Zircon crystals take in uranium as they grow but reject lead, so lead found inside a zircon came from the decay of uranium after the crystal formed.

Radiometric dating measures the last time a rock was melted or disturbed enough to reset its radioactive elements; most fossils cannot be dated this way, so geologists date volcanic ash or other igneous rocks that crystallized from molten rock.

title: The oldest crystals on Earth
description: Earth's first rocks have been recycled by plate tectonics, but tough zircon grains from the Jack Hills of Western Australia survive from about 4.4 billion years ago.

facts.text: Scientists cannot date Earth's formation directly from Earth rocks because Earth's oldest rocks have been recycled and destroyed by plate tectonics.
Zircon crystals from the Jack Hills of Western Australia, found in much younger sedimentary rock, crystallized about 4.4 billion years ago; they are the oldest known material formed on Earth.
Zircon is highly resistant to chemical alteration and abrasion, so its grains can survive several cycles of weathering, erosion and deposition for billions of years.

title: Dating Earth with meteorites
description: Earth formed with the rest of the Solar System, so meteorites, primitive leftovers dated to 4.53 to 4.58 billion years, help fix Earth's age at about 4.54 billion years.

facts.text: Scientists date Earth by assuming it formed at the same time as the Solar System's other solid bodies; meteorites, primitive fragments of asteroids, give the best ages, and more than 70 of them date to between 4.53 and 4.58 billion years ago.

The best age for Earth, 4.54 billion years with an uncertainty of less than 1 percent, comes from comparing lead isotopes, changed over time by uranium decay, in Earth's oldest lead ores with nearly uranium-free lead in iron meteorites such as Canyon Diablo.

title: The geologic time scale
description: Geologists divide Earth's history into eons, eras, periods, epochs and ages, with boundaries set mostly by fossils. The Phanerozoic, the eon of visible life, is only the last eighth.

facts.text: The geologic time scale divides Earth's history into named units, from longest to shortest: eons, eras, periods, epochs and ages; the International Commission on Stratigraphy maintains the standard International Chronostratigraphic Chart.
Earth's history is divided into four eons: the Hadean, Archean, Proterozoic and Phanerozoic.

The Phanerozoic, the eon of visible life, covers only about the last one-eighth of the time since Earth's crust formed; its three eras are the Paleozoic (541 to 252 million years ago), the Mesozoic (252 to 66 million years ago) and the Cenozoic (66 million years ago to today).
Fossils are the chief means of setting up the geologic time scale: the appearance and disappearance of widespread species in the rock record mark the beginnings and ends of its intervals.

title: Where humans sit in deep time
description: Homo sapiens appeared about 300,000 years ago, in the Cenozoic Era's Quaternary Period. On a one-day clock of Earth's history, that is the last few seconds.

facts.text: Homo sapiens evolved in Africa about 300,000 years ago.
The present lies in the Phanerozoic Eon's Cenozoic Era, in the Quaternary Period and its Holocene Epoch.

title: The Great Oxidation Event
description: Cyanobacteria released oxygen by photosynthesis, and about 2.4 billion years ago oxygen in the air rose sharply. Stromatolites record these early microbes.

facts.text: Oxygen did not make up a significant part of Earth's atmosphere until after the Great Oxidation Event.
Cyanobacteria (once called blue-green algae) use photosynthesis to turn carbon dioxide and water into carbohydrates, releasing free oxygen.
The Great Oxidation Event, when oxygen in the atmosphere rose sharply, happened about 2.4 billion years ago.

Stromatolites are layered deposits, mainly limestone, built by blue-green algae (cyanobacteria); some of Earth's first life is recorded in stromatolites 3.5 billion years old, and living ones grow in Shark Bay, Western Australia.

title: Banded iron: oxygen rusts the sea
description: Oxygen from microbes combined with iron dissolved in the early oceans, and the iron oxide settled as red bands. Only when the iron ran out could oxygen fill the air.

facts.text: Oxygen made by ocean bacteria combined with iron dissolved in seawater to form insoluble iron oxide, which sank and laid red iron-oxide sheets between silica-rich layers; once the dissolved iron was used up, oxygen escaped into the atmosphere.
Banded iron formations consist of iron oxides, chiefly hematite, alternating with chert or quartz; most are older than 1.7 billion years, and they are used as iron ore.

title: The supercontinent cycle
description: Continents gather into a supercontinent, split apart as new oceans open, then drift back together as old ocean floor sinks by subduction, every 300 to 500 million years.

facts.text: A supercontinent is a landmass holding the vast majority of Earth's land; supercontinents form, break up and re-form in a cycle lasting about 300 to 500 million years, driven largely by convection in Earth's mantle.
When a supercontinent breaks up, oceans open between the pieces; later, subduction of oceanic plates draws the continental fragments back together.

title: Supercontinents past and future
description: Before Pangaea came Rodinia and Columbia (Nuna); scientists project another supercontinent in about 250 million years.

facts.text: Past supercontinents include Columbia (also called Nuna), about 2.1 to 1.8 billion years ago, and Rodinia, about 1.2 billion to 750 million years ago; Pangaea assembled about 299 to 273 million years ago.
Scientists project that a new supercontinent will form in about 250 million years; proposals include Pangaea Proxima, Amasia and Aurica.

title: How coal formed
description: Plants in ancient swampy forests piled up as peat, and burial slowly heated and squeezed it into lignite, bituminous coal and anthracite.

facts.text: Coal is a combustible sedimentary rock formed from plants that lived hundreds of millions of years ago in swampy forests; covered by layers of dirt and rock, the plants were turned into coal by pressure and heat over millions of years.

Plant matter accumulating in warm, humid, swampy regions first becomes peat; with deeper burial and rising temperature it turns over millions of years into lignite, subbituminous coal, bituminous coal and anthracite.
A coal's rank depends on how much heat and pressure acted on the plants; anthracite, the highest rank, contains 86% to 97% carbon, while bituminous coal contains 45% to 86%.
The Carboniferous Period, which began about 358.9 million years ago, is named for the coal-bearing rock layers typical of that time.

title: How oil and gas formed
description: Tiny marine plants and animals were buried under sand, silt and rock, and heat and pressure turned them into oil and natural gas, much of it in organic-rich black shale.

facts.text: Crude oil formed from the remains of tiny marine plants and animals, such as diatoms, covered by layers of sand, silt and rock; heat and pressure turned the remains into oil over millions of years.

Natural gas formed from plant and animal remains buried under sand, silt and rock; pressure and heat changed some of this material into coal, some into oil and some into natural gas, and some gas moved into cracks and spaces in overlying rock.
Shale forms when silt- and clay-size particles are compacted, and black shale contains organic material that can generate oil and natural gas.

title: Bracketing a fossil's age
description: Most fossils can't be dated directly, but radiometric dates on volcanic ash above and below a fossil layer pin its age between them.

facts.text: Dating volcanic ash layers above and below a fossil-bearing layer brackets the fossils' age: in one example, trilobites came out older than 520 but younger than 545 million years; dates like these built the geologic time scale.

title: What air is made of
description: Dry air is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen, with almost 1% argon; water vapor varies. Nitrogen piles up because almost nothing removes it.

facts.text: Dry air is about 78% nitrogen (78.08%), 21% oxygen (20.95%) and 0.93% argon, so nitrogen and oxygen together make up about 99% of it; water vapor varies from about 0 to 4% of the air.
Nitrogen is almost completely chemically inert in the atmosphere, is relatively insoluble in water and does not condense out like water vapor, so it has built up to become 78% of the air.
Oxygen became the second most abundant gas in the air through photosynthesis, in which living things use water, carbon dioxide and sunlight and release oxygen.

title: Tiny gases, big effects
description: Carbon dioxide is only about 0.04% of the air, about 4 molecules in 10,000, yet greenhouse gases like it have a huge effect on climate.

facts.text: NOAA's global monthly mean carbon dioxide was 427.62 ppm in June 2026: about 428 parts per million, roughly 0.04% of the air, or about 4 in every 10,000 molecules.
Only a tiny share of the gases in the atmosphere are greenhouse gases, such as carbon dioxide and water vapor, but they have a huge effect on climate; nitrogen and oxygen cannot absorb heat.

title: The layers of the atmosphere
description: Temperature falls through the troposphere, rises through the stratosphere, falls through the mesosphere and rises again in the thermosphere.

facts.text: The troposphere, the lowest layer, reaches up to about 10 km; nearly all weather happens there because it holds 99% of the atmosphere's water vapor, and it gets colder as you climb.
The mesosphere reaches up to about 85 km; temperatures fall again as you rise through it, reaching the atmosphere's coldest, about -90 °C, near its top, and most meteors burn up there.
The thermosphere absorbs high-energy X-rays and ultraviolet light from the Sun, heating it to hundreds or at times thousands of degrees, but its air is so thin it would feel freezing cold to us.
National Weather Service weather balloons report pressure, temperature and humidity every second and can rise past 35 km; a flight can last more than two hours.

title: Why the stratosphere warms with height
description: Ozone in the stratosphere absorbs the Sun's ultraviolet light and turns it into heat, so the stratosphere gets warmer the higher you go, and stays calm.

facts.text: The stratosphere reaches up to about 50 km and holds the ozone layer; ozone absorbs high-energy ultraviolet light and converts it into heat, so the stratosphere gets warmer with height.
Because temperature rises with height in the stratosphere, its air lacks the turbulence and updrafts of the troposphere, and passenger jets fly in its lower part partly for the smoother ride.

title: Air pressure is the weight of the air
description: Air pressure is the push of the whole column of air above you, about 14.7 pounds per square inch at sea level, balanced by an equal push outward.

facts.text: Atmospheric pressure is the force per unit area exerted by the column of air above a place; standard sea-level pressure is 1,013.25 millibars (about 1,013).
Average sea-level pressure is about 14.7 pounds on every square inch; an equal force pushing outward keeps us from being crushed.

title: Why pressure drops with height
description: Gravity packs the air densest near the ground, so pressure falls as you climb: half of all the air lies within about 5.6 km of the surface.

facts.text: Gravity pulls the atmosphere's mass toward the surface, so pressure and air density are greatest at the bottom and decrease with height; half of the atmosphere's mass lies within the first 5.6 km.
A National Weather Service weather balloon is about 1.5 m wide at launch, gradually expands as it rises and bursts when it reaches 6 to 8 m across.
Mount Everest, the tallest mountain on the planet, is only about 9 km high, inside the troposphere.
Air molecules are spaced farther apart at higher altitudes, so there is less oxygen to breathe at the top of a high mountain than at sea level.

title: Rising air cools as it expands
description: Air rising into lower pressure expands and spends its own internal energy, so it cools without losing heat; sinking air is squeezed and warms.

facts.text: A rising parcel of air meets lower pressure and expands; expanding uses its own internal energy, so it cools without exchanging heat with its surroundings (adiabatic cooling), as air rushing out of a tire valve feels cool.
Sinking air meets rising pressure and is squeezed into a smaller volume, and the work done on it raises its temperature (adiabatic warming).
Dry air cools as it rises, and warms as it sinks, at the dry adiabatic lapse rate of 9.8 °C per kilometer, about 10 °C per km (1 °C per 100 m).

title: Why mountaintops are cold
description: On average the air cools about 6.5 °C for every 1,000 m you climb, so a 27 °C sea-level day is about 1 °C at 4,000 m.

facts.text: Near the surface, air temperature falls on average by about 6.5 °C for every 1,000 m climbed (the standard lapse rate), so 27 °C at sea level means about 1 °C at 4,000 m.

title: How CFCs thinned the ozone layer
description: CFCs are so stable they drift up to the stratosphere, where ultraviolet light frees chlorine; each chlorine atom can destroy over 100,000 ozone molecules.

facts.text: In May 1985, British Antarctic Survey scientists reported in Nature that by 1984 the ozone layer over Halley station in Antarctica was only about two-thirds as thick as in earlier decades; CFCs from aerosol cans and fridges were blamed.

CFCs are not broken down in the lower atmosphere, so they drift into the stratosphere over two to five years; there intense ultraviolet light breaks them apart, releasing chlorine atoms, and one chlorine atom can destroy over 100,000 ozone molecules.

The extra ultraviolet light that passes through the ozone hole cannot explain the warming of Earth's surface; the ozone hole's role in global warming is small compared with the impact of human activities.
The Antarctic ozone "hole" that forms each southern spring is not a hole through the layer but a large area of the stratosphere with extremely low amounts of ozone.

title: The Montreal Protocol
description: Signed in 1987, the Montreal Protocol phased out about 99% of ozone-depleting chemicals; the ozone layer should recover by around 2040 to 2066.

facts.text: The Montreal Protocol, signed in 1987, is a global agreement to protect the ozone layer by phasing out the production and consumption of the chemicals that deplete it.
The Montreal Protocol has achieved universal ratification, with 198 parties, and has led to the phase-out of 99 per cent of ozone-depleting substances.
With continued compliance, ozone is expected to return to 1980 values around 2066 over Antarctica, around 2045 over the Arctic and around 2040 across the rest of the globe.
Because ozone-depleting chemicals last a long time in the atmosphere, it will take decades for the ozone hole to recover.

title: Why the sky is blue
description: Air molecules, far smaller than light waves, scatter short blue waves much more than long red ones (Rayleigh scattering), filling the sky with blue.

facts.text: The Moon has no atmosphere, so its sky is black both night and day, as photographs from the Apollo Moon landings show.
Sunlight looks white but is made of many colors, each with a different wavelength: red has the longest, blue and violet much shorter; a prism bends the light, while air molecules scatter it.

Sunlight entering the atmosphere meets gas molecules, mainly nitrogen and oxygen, much smaller than the wavelength of light; they scatter shorter wavelengths much more than longer ones (Rayleigh scattering), so the sky looks blue.
Violet light is scattered even more than blue, but our eyes are more sensitive to blue and sunlight contains less violet, so the sky looks blue rather than purple.

title: Why sunsets turn red
description: A low Sun's light crosses much more air, so the blue is scattered away and reds and oranges come through; blue sky and red sunset are one process.

facts.text: At sunrise and sunset, sunlight passes through a thicker layer of atmosphere, so more of the blue is scattered away and the longer red and orange wavelengths reach your eyes; blue skies and red sunsets come from the same scattering.
Small particles of dust, pollution and other aerosols also scatter blue light, which can make sunsets a deeper red.

title: Light in, infrared out
description: Sunlight mostly passes through the air to warm the surface; the warm surface gives off thermal infrared, and greenhouse gases catch and re-send that heat.

facts.text: About 48 percent of incoming sunlight, roughly half, passes through the atmosphere and is absorbed by the surface; the warmed Earth gives off energy as thermal infrared radiation, like the heat you feel from a heat lamp.

Greenhouse gas molecules that absorb infrared later release it; some heads to space, some is absorbed by another greenhouse gas molecule and some returns to the surface, which keeps heat near Earth's surface.

title: Why only some gases trap heat
description: Two-atom molecules like nitrogen and oxygen only stretch in and out without shifting their charge, so they cannot absorb infrared; molecules of three or more atoms can.

facts.text: Two-atom molecules such as nitrogen (N2) and oxygen (O2) vibrate only by moving closer together and apart, while molecules of three or more atoms vibrate in more complex patterns; that is why carbon dioxide, water vapor and methane absorb infrared and nitrogen and oxygen do not.

A molecule made of two identical atoms, like nitrogen or oxygen, cannot create an uneven electric charge as it vibrates, so it cannot absorb infrared; carbon dioxide and water vapor vibrations do shift their charge.

title: Earth's energy budget
description: About 29% of sunlight is reflected; Earth's temperature holds steady when absorbed sunlight equals heat radiated away, and a warmer Earth sheds heat faster.

facts.text: About 29 percent of the solar energy reaching the top of the atmosphere is reflected back to space by clouds, particles in the air and bright surfaces like snow and ice; about 71 percent is absorbed.

When incoming solar energy is balanced by an equal flow of heat to space, Earth is in radiative equilibrium and global temperature is stable; anything that changes incoming or outgoing energy makes temperatures rise or fall.
Rising concentrations of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases decrease the heat radiated to space, pushing the energy budget out of balance.

As Earth's surface warms, the heat it radiates to space rises quickly; this is the main thing that prevents runaway heating, and once greenhouse gases stop rising the climate settles into balance at a higher temperature.

title: Albedo: how reflective a surface is
description: Albedo runs from 0 (absorbs everything) to 1 (reflects everything): open ocean reflects about 6% of sunlight, snow-covered ice up to 90%.

facts.text: Albedo measures how well a surface reflects sunlight, from 0 (absorbs all) to 1 (reflects all); open ocean reflects about 6 percent, snow-covered ice as much as 90 percent, and dark blacktop absorbs more sunlight than lighter concrete.

title: Why moving air curves
description: Earth's surface moves faster at the Equator than near the poles, so air moving north or south appears to curve as the ground shifts under it: the Coriolis effect.

facts.text: Earth completes a rotation every 24 hours, so the wide Equator moves at nearly 1,600 km/h while places near the poles barely move; air keeps its own motion while the ground beneath moves at a different speed, so its path appears to curve, with no real force involved.
A ball rolled across a spinning merry-go-round appears to curve, but someone on the ground sees it travel in a straight line: the riders move out of its path while it rolls.
You cannot see the Coriolis effect in a flushing toilet or a draining pool; the swirl depends on the basin's design or outside forces.

title: Why storms spin
description: Air rushing into a low-pressure storm is deflected, so storms turn counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern; the effect vanishes at the Equator.

facts.text: Air pulled into a low-pressure storm from all directions is deflected (to the right in the Northern Hemisphere, to the left in the Southern), so storms rotate counterclockwise in the north and clockwise in the south.
The Coriolis effect is strongest near the poles and absent at the Equator; because cyclones need it to circulate, hurricanes almost never form in equatorial regions and never cross the Equator.

title: A planet always changing
description: Earth is about 4.54 billion years old and its plates creep 2 to 15 cm a year; given deep time, slow changes remake the planet while the air changes fast.

facts.text: The best age for the Earth is 4.54 billion years, based on lead isotopes in ancient lead ores and meteorites.
Tectonic plates move relative to each other at 2 to 15 cm a year, roughly as fast as fingernails grow; at 2 cm a year a plate travels 20 km in a million years.

title: How much water vapor air can hold
description: Warmer air can hold more water vapor; relative humidity compares the vapor present with the most the air could hold at that temperature, so cooling air raises it.

facts.text: The most water vapor air can hold depends on temperature: warmer air can hold more, which is why the muggiest days usually come at the height of summer heat.
Water vapor, the gas form of water, is invisible and is in the air around us all the time.
After a hot shower the air in a bathroom holds more water vapor, and vapor that touches the cooler mirror condenses back into liquid water.
Relative humidity compares the water vapor in the air with the most it could hold at that temperature: half the maximum is 50%, and the maximum is 100%, when the air is saturated.

title: The dew point
description: The dew point is the temperature at which air, cooled with its moisture unchanged, becomes saturated and its water vapor starts to condense.

facts.text: The dew point is the temperature to which air must be cooled, with its moisture unchanged, to become saturated; then water vapor condenses into liquid droplets.
Dew or frost forms on grass, often early in the morning, when the surface cools to the dew point.
The dew point is a measure of how much moisture the air contains; high dew points, common in spring and summer, mean very humid conditions.

title: Why clouds form
description: Air that is lifted expands and cools; when it cools to its dew point, its water vapor condenses into tiny droplets that make a cloud.

facts.text: When air rises, the pressure around it drops, so it expands and cools; when it cools to its dew point, water vapor condenses into droplets and a cloud forms.
Cloud droplets are only about a hundredth of a millimeter across, small and light enough to stay up in the air.

Air is lifted into clouds in a few main ways: sun-warmed air rising from the ground, wind forced up a slope, winds meeting in a low with nowhere to go but up, and air pushed up at weather fronts; all cloud types form by these processes.

title: Condensation nuclei
description: Water vapor condenses far more easily onto tiny particles such as dust, pollen, smoke and sea salt; without them, air would need a relative humidity well over 100% to form droplets.

facts.text: Water vapor condenses much more easily when it has a particle to condense on; these tiny particles, such as dust, pollen, smoke and sea salt, are called condensation nuclei.
Most condensation nuclei come from fires over land and from wave action over the oceans, which throws sea salt into the air.
Without such particles, air would need a relative humidity well over 100% before cloud droplets could form; they are abundant in the air, so clouds rarely lack them.

title: Cumulus, stratus and cirrus
description: Clouds are named from Luke Howard's 1802 Latin system: cumulus heaps, stratus layers and cirrus wisps, with nimbus meaning rain-bearing.

facts.text: Luke Howard, a London pharmacist and amateur meteorologist, proposed classifying clouds in 1802, sorting them into three main types (cumulus, stratus and cirrus); we largely use his system today.

Cloud names come from Latin: cumulus means heaped up and puffy, stratus flat and layered, cirrus high and wispy (the word is Latin for a curl of hair), and nimbus rain-bearing, so nimbostratus is a flat, rain-bearing cloud.
The World Meteorological Organization extends Howard's system to 10 main cloud groups, sorted into low, medium and high clouds.
Cumulus clouds are puffy white clouds like floating cotton balls, with flat bases; they can go with fair or stormy weather, and cauliflower-like tops warn of showers.
Stratus clouds are low, uniform gray layers that can cover the whole sky, like fog that doesn't reach the ground, sometimes with light mist or drizzle.

title: What clouds say about the weather
description: Cloud shape and height hint at the weather: high icy cirrus that thickens can signal a warm front, towering cumulonimbus bring thunderstorms and gray nimbostratus bring steady rain or snow.

facts.text: Cirrus clouds are thin, wispy streamers made of ice crystals high in the sky, often seen in fair weather; if they thicken and are followed by cirrostratus, a warm front may be on the way.
If a cloud forms high enough, where the air is cold enough, it is made of tiny ice crystals instead of droplets and looks thin and wispy.
Cumulus clouds form when sunshine heats the ground, the ground warms the air above it, and that air rises and cools.
Cumulus clouds can grow into cumulonimbus clouds, which produce thunderstorms.
Nimbostratus clouds are dark gray, low and ragged, and bring continuous rain or snow.

title: How cloud droplets become rain
description: Cloud droplets must grow about a million-fold to fall; outside the tropics, ice does most of the growing, while warm tropical clouds rain by collision and merging.

facts.text: In the middle latitudes, rain generally starts out as snow or ice high in the cloud, even in summer, and melts as it falls through warmer air below.
For rain to form, cloud droplets must grow more than a million times in mass (about a million droplets make one raindrop), and condensation alone is far too slow to do it.

In warm clouds, whose tops are above freezing, bigger droplets fall through smaller ones, collide and merge until they are heavy enough to fall; tropical rain forms this way, and strong updrafts let drops grow big fast into heavy rain.

title: The ice crystal (Bergeron) process
description: In clouds with supercooled droplets and ice crystals together, the ice grows by taking water vapor while the droplets evaporate; the crystals become snowflakes that fall and often melt into rain.

facts.text: Many clouds contain supercooled water: droplets that stay liquid below freezing, mixed with ice crystals.
In such mixed clouds, water vapor deposits onto ice crystals more readily than onto liquid droplets, so the crystals grow while the droplets evaporate to feed them; this is the Bergeron process.
Ice crystals join into snowflakes that fall once heavy enough; if they fall through above-freezing air below the cloud, they melt and reach the ground as rain.
The six-fold symmetry of a snow crystal comes from the way water molecules are arranged in the ice crystal lattice.
Snow crystals grow straight from water vapor into ice, and snowflakes can be considered minerals: solid, naturally occurring, crystalline and inorganic.

title: Highs and lows
description: In a low, winds meet and air rises into clouds and rain; in a high, air sinks and spreads out, holding back clouds and bringing settled weather.

facts.text: Weather maps mark areas of high pressure with a blue H and areas of low pressure with a red L; lows tend to bring clouds and storms, highs calm, sunny weather.
Winds blow away from areas of high pressure and toward areas of low pressure.
In a low-pressure system, winds blow in toward the center and the air rises where they meet; as it rises, its water vapor condenses into clouds and often rain or snow.
In a high-pressure system, air from higher up sinks and spreads outward at the surface; the sinking air reduces cloud formation, so highs bring settled weather with light winds.
A high can become stationary for a long time, a pattern called a block, bringing prolonged dry, settled weather and, in summer, heatwaves and droughts.

title: How winds circle highs and lows
description: North of the Equator, winds spiral counterclockwise into lows and clockwise out of highs; the Coriolis effect bends them, and south of the Equator the directions reverse.

facts.text: Because of Earth's spin (the Coriolis effect), winds swirl counterclockwise around a low and clockwise around a high north of the Equator, and the other way around south of it.

title: Air masses
description: An air mass is a huge body of air with fairly uniform temperature and humidity, which takes on the character of the place it forms and carries it elsewhere.

facts.text: An air mass is a large volume of air that is mostly uniform in temperature and moisture, and it can extend thousands of kilometers.
An air mass takes on the features of the region where it forms, such as heat or cold and dryness or moisture, and winds carry those conditions to new regions.
An air mass changes as it moves: cold continental polar air that moves over warmer ocean warms up and picks up moisture evaporating from the sea.
Cold and warm air masses usually come together in the middle latitudes, such as over the United States, where they form weather fronts and can produce big storms.

title: Naming air masses
description: An air mass's name gives where it formed: maritime (humid, over ocean) or continental (drier, over land), and tropical (warm) or polar and arctic (cold).

facts.text: Maritime air masses form over oceans and are more humid; continental ones form over land and are drier; tropical ones are warm, and polar or arctic ones are cold.
Over North America, cold, dry continental polar air flows south from northern Canada and the Arctic, while warm, moist air flows north from the Gulf of Mexico.

title: Cold fronts
description: At a cold front, dense cold air pushes under warm air and forces it up quickly, bringing sudden storms, a temperature drop and then clearer, cooler air.

facts.text: A weather front is the boundary at Earth's surface between two air masses with different temperature and humidity; when a front passes, the weather changes.
At a cold front, a cold air mass pushes into warmer air; the denser cold air pushes under the lighter warm air and forces it up, producing cumulus or cumulonimbus clouds and thunderstorms.
As a cold front passes, winds become gusty, the temperature drops suddenly and heavy rain can fall; pressure changes from falling to rising, and afterward it is cooler with clearing skies.
Cold fronts move up to twice as fast as warm fronts, because it is hard for warm air to push dense cold air across the ground.

title: Warm fronts
description: At a warm front, warm air slides up over cooler air; high cirrus come first, then the clouds lower and rain becomes likely.

facts.text: At a warm front, warm air pushes into cooler air and rises over it; clouds form in the warm air high above, so high cirrus and cirrostratus often come first, then the clouds lower and rain becomes likely.
On weather maps, a cold front is a blue line with triangles and a warm front a red line with semicircles; the shapes point the way the front is moving.

title: Three circulation cells
description: Because Earth spins, each hemisphere's air circulates in three cells (Hadley, Ferrel and polar), with the stormy polar front where warm and cold air meet.

facts.text: If Earth didn't spin, each hemisphere would have one large circulation cell from the Equator to the pole; because it spins, the Coriolis effect splits the circulation into three cells north and three south of the Equator.
The Ferrel cell, in the middle latitudes, acts like a gear between the Hadley and polar cells; its surface winds, turned by the Coriolis effect, blow mostly from the west (the westerlies).
The polar cells are the smallest and weakest: air sinks over the poles and flows toward lower latitudes at the surface.
Where warm air carried poleward by the Ferrel cell meets cold polar air, generally between 60 and 70 degrees, air rises along the polar front and low pressure forms, bringing unsettled weather.
Together, the three cells act like a giant conveyor belt that carries heat from the tropics toward the poles.

title: The ITCZ and the Hadley cell
description: Trade winds meet near the Equator and rise in thunderstorms (the ITCZ, or doldrums); the air sinks over the subtropics, making highs and deserts.

facts.text: In the Hadley cells, trade winds meet near the Equator and rise in a broken line of thunderstorms, the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ); air then flows poleward aloft and sinks over the subtropics, making high pressure over hot deserts such as the Sahara.
The Hadley cells are the largest, reaching from the Equator to between 30 and 40 degrees north and south.
Sailors call the ITCZ the doldrums: because the air there moves mostly upward, there is often little surface wind, and it can becalm sailing ships for weeks.

title: The jet stream
description: Jet streams are fast west-to-east winds high in the troposphere that form where warm and cold air meet, and blow hardest in winter.

facts.text: Japanese meteorologist Wasaburo Ooishi first documented the jet stream in the 1920s, using weather balloons launched from Japan that were carried out over the Pacific.
Jet streams are bands of strong wind about 5 to 9 miles (about 8 to 14 km) above the ground that generally blow from west to east.
Jet streams average about 110 miles per hour (about 180 km/h) and can reach 250 miles per hour (about 400 km/h) or more.
Jet streams form where warm air masses meet cold ones; the bigger the temperature difference, the stronger the winds.
Jet streams are faster in winter, when the temperature differences between warm and cold air masses are greatest.

title: How the jet stream steers weather
description: The jet stream carries storms and lows along, usually west to east; when it meanders, weather systems can stall.

facts.text: Jet streams carry weather systems along, so most storms don't sit over one place; the polar front jet steers low-pressure systems, usually from west to east.
When the jet stream runs straight from west to east, weather systems move through quickly; when it meanders north and south, systems can stall, bringing long spells of rain and wind.
Jet streams blow at about the height airliners fly: a plane heading the same way gets a boost and saves fuel, so pilots flying west try to avoid a strong jet.

title: A low and its fronts
