description: A mid-latitude low carries a warm front on its east side and a faster cold front behind; when the cold front catches up, it forms an occluded front.

facts.text: Warm fronts often form on the east side of low-pressure systems, where warmer air from the south is pushed north.
Because cold fronts move faster, a cold front can catch up with the warm front ahead of it and lift the warm air off the ground, forming an occluded front, usually near the center of a low.

title: The three stages of a thunderstorm
description: A thunderstorm cell grows in an updraft (developing), rains and flashes with updraft and downdraft side by side (mature), then dies when its rain-cooled downdraft cuts off the warm, moist air feeding it (dissipating).

facts.text: A single thunderstorm cell lives about 30 to 60 minutes and has three distinct stages: developing, mature and dissipating.
In the developing stage, a rising column of air (an updraft) pushes a cumulus cloud upward into a towering cumulus, with little to no rain.

As warm, moist air rises in an updraft, its moisture condenses into water droplets and the cumulus cloud grows; raindrops fall when the rising air can no longer hold them up, and a downdraft pulls water down as rain.

A thunderstorm turns mature when precipitation falls out of it and creates a downdraft while the updraft still feeds the storm; it often reaches 12 to 18 km high, and hail, heavy rain, frequent lightning, strong winds and tornadoes are most likely then.

In the dissipating stage the downdraft overcomes the updraft; the gust front of rain-cooled air cuts off the warm, moist air feeding the storm, and light rain may linger before only the anvil top remains.

title: Where a storm's water vapor comes from
description: Most of the water vapor in the air evaporates from oceans, lakes and rivers, but about a tenth is transpired by plants.

facts.text: About 90 percent of the water in the atmosphere is produced by evaporation from water bodies, and the other 10 percent comes from transpiration from plants.

title: How a storm charges up for lightning
description: In the updraft, rising ice crystals collide with graupel: crystals turn positive and are carried to the top, graupel turns negative and stays lower. When the charge difference beats the air's insulation, lightning discharges; thunder follows.

facts.text: Air moving within a thunderstorm cloud builds up electric charges, allowing lightning to form in much the same way you can make a spark after shuffling your feet on a carpet.

The main charging zone is in the updraft at about -15 to -25 °C, among supercooled droplets, small ice crystals and graupel (soft hail); when rising ice crystals collide with graupel, the crystals become positively charged and the graupel negatively charged.

The updraft carries the positively charged ice crystals to the top of the storm, while the heavier graupel stays in the middle or falls lower, so the top of the cloud becomes positive and the middle to lower part negative; the ground beneath turns positively charged.

Air acts as an insulator between the charges in a cloud and between cloud and ground; when the charge difference becomes too great, that insulation breaks down in a rapid discharge of electricity: lightning.
You see lightning almost immediately, but thunder takes about 5 seconds to travel a mile, and it can be heard only about 10 miles from the strike.
There is no safe place outside when thunderstorms are nearby; if you hear thunder, you are likely within striking distance, so "When Thunder Roars, Go Indoors!"

title: Fulgurites: glass made by lightning
description: Lightning that strikes quartz sand can melt it into a fulgurite, a glass tube, because the melt cools too fast for crystals to grow.

facts.text: Fulgurites are natural tubes or crusts of glass formed when lightning fuses silica (quartz) sand or rock; sand fulgurite tubes are glassy inside because the sand cools and solidifies rapidly, and they turn up in clean, dry beach and desert sand.

title: How hail grows and falls
description: Updrafts lift frozen drops through supercooled water, which freezes onto them; the stronger the updraft, the bigger the stone, and it falls when the updraft can no longer hold it.

facts.text: Updrafts carry raindrops into extremely cold parts of a thunderstorm; hailstones grow by colliding with supercooled water (liquid below freezing), which freezes on contact, and strong updrafts keep lifting them, so the stronger the updraft, the larger the hail.
Hail falls when the updraft can no longer support the weight of the ice or the updraft weakens.

Florida has the most thunderstorms in the US, but the area where Nebraska, Colorado and Wyoming meet usually has the most hailstorms, because the freezing level over the high plains is much closer to the ground, leaving hail less time to melt as it falls.

title: Reading a hailstone's layers
description: Milky layers freeze fast (dry growth) and trap air bubbles; clear layers freeze slowly (wet growth) and let bubbles escape, so a cut hailstone records its trip.

facts.text: In dry growth (air well below freezing) droplets freeze instantly on a hailstone and trap air bubbles: milky ice. In wet growth (just below freezing, lots of water) water freezes slowly and bubbles escape: clear ice. Counting layers hints at trips through the storm.

title: Supercells: storms with a rotating updraft
description: A supercell has a deep, persistent rotating updraft (a mesocyclone). Shear tilts it so updraft and downdraft stay apart, it can last hours, and it makes the biggest hail and almost all violent tornadoes.

facts.text: On July 23, 2010, a supercell thunderstorm dropped the US record hailstone at Vivian, South Dakota: 8 inches (20 cm) across and weighing about 1.94 pounds.

What makes a supercell unique among thunderstorms is a deep and persistent rotating updraft called a mesocyclone; wind shear also tilts the storm, keeping its updraft and downdraft apart, and a supercell can last for several hours.

The vast majority of significant tornadoes (EF2 and stronger) and virtually all violent tornadoes (EF4 to EF5) come from supercell thunderstorms, though scientists are still studying exactly how tornadoes form.

title: How wind shear starts a storm spinning
description: Winds that change speed or direction with height set the air rolling sideways; a strong updraft draws that spin in and tips it upright, so the updraft rotates.

facts.text: Changes in wind speed and direction with height (wind shear), such as southeast winds at the surface and faster southwest winds aloft, give the air horizontal spin, like a football; when a storm's updraft draws that air in, the updraft rotates.

title: Why the central US gets so many tornadoes
description: Flat land that heats quickly, Gulf of Mexico moisture and cooler air from the north feed frequent severe storms, though why some storms make tornadoes is still not fully understood.

facts.text: The United States averages around 1,200 tornadoes a year, give or take a few hundred.

The central US has a large, fairly flat core (the Great Plains and Mississippi River valley) that heats up quickly much of the year; moisture from the Gulf of Mexico and the region's plants meets cooler air from the Upper Great Plains and Canada, feeding frequent severe thunderstorms.

The classic answer, warm moist Gulf air meeting cold Canadian air and dry air from the Rockies, is an oversimplification: most thunderstorms in those conditions never make tornadoes, and scientists do not fully understand why some do.

title: The Enhanced Fujita (EF) scale
description: Since 2007 US tornadoes are rated after the fact from surveyed damage; the EF0 to EF5 wind speeds are estimates, so a tornado over open country can rate low.

facts.text: Since February 1, 2007, the US EF scale has rated tornadoes from damage: NWS surveyors match it to 28 damage indicators (barns to schools) and 8 degrees of damage, rating the strongest wind in the path; the winds are estimates, and true ground-level winds are rarely known.
On the EF scale, EF0 means estimated 3-second gusts of 65 to 85 mph and EF5 means gusts over 200 mph.

Part of the Bridge Creek-Moore, Oklahoma, tornado of 3 May 1999, which did F5 damage elsewhere, was rated only F2 to F3 across a sparsely built valley, possibly because there were few substantial buildings to judge its strength by.

title: A hurricane's eye
description: The eye is a roughly circular area of fair weather at the center, with the lowest surface pressure and slowly sinking air; most are 20 to 40 miles across.

facts.text: The eye of a hurricane is a roughly circular area of fair weather at its center, with the lowest surface pressure; eyes range from 5 to 120 miles across, but most are 20 to 40 miles; the air in the eye sinks slowly, and exactly how the eye forms is still debated.

title: The eyewall and rain bands
description: Around the eye, a ring of towering thunderstorms (the eyewall) holds the highest winds and heaviest rain; long spiral rain bands lie farther out. Eyewall updrafts are too weak for much lightning.

facts.text: Hurricanes run on warm, moist air from evaporating ocean water; the air rises, cools, and its water vapor condenses into droplets that build big cumulonimbus clouds.
The eyewall is a ring of deep convection (towering thunderstorms) bordering the eye, with the highest surface winds in the storm, and more rain falls around the eyewall than in the outer rain bands.

Little lightning occurs in a hurricane's inner core, because the eyewall's relatively weak updrafts lack the supercooled water needed to charge up a thunderstorm; lightning is more common in the outer rain bands.

Spiral bands are long, narrow bands of rain and thunderstorms, lined up with the wind, that spiral into the center of a hurricane; a region of lighter rain between the eyewall and an outer band, called the moat, appears in some storms.

title: What a hurricane category measures
description: The Saffir-Simpson category (1 to 5) rates only maximum sustained wind; it leaves out storm surge, rain flooding and tornadoes, which storms of any category can bring.

facts.text: The Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale rates hurricanes 1 to 5 based only on maximum sustained wind speed and estimates property damage; Category 1 is 74 to 95 mph, Category 5 is 157 mph or higher, and Category 3 and up are major hurricanes.
The Saffir-Simpson scale does not take into account storm surge, rainfall flooding or tornadoes, and hurricanes of all categories can produce all three, including deadly rain-induced floods.

title: Water, not wind, is the big hurricane killer
description: Most US hurricane deaths come from water, with rain flooding leading; rainfall depends on a storm's speed, size and terrain, not its category.

facts.text: A study of direct US deaths from Atlantic tropical cyclones from 1963 to 2024 found about 80 percent came from water (freshwater flooding 36 percent, storm surge 33 percent) and about 13 percent from wind and tornadoes.

Rainfall from a tropical cyclone depends not on its strength but on its speed and size and the local geography: slower, larger storms produce more rain, and mountains enhance it; flooding is the major threat for people living inland.

title: Nor'easters
description: East Coast storms named for their northeast coastal winds, most common September to April, fueled by the contrast between cold continental air and air warmed over the Atlantic.

facts.text: A nor'easter is an East Coast storm named for its typically northeast coastal winds; it can occur any time of year but is most frequent and violent from September to April, usually forms within 100 miles of the coast between Georgia and New Jersey, and peaks near New England.

In winter the polar jet stream carries cold Arctic air across Canada and the US toward the Atlantic, where the warm Gulf Stream keeps coastal waters mild; the temperature difference between cold air over land and warmer air over the water fuels nor'easters.
Nor'easters nearly always bring heavy rain or snow, gale-force winds and rough seas, and occasionally coastal flooding; the crowded Washington to Boston I-95 corridor is especially affected.

title: What makes a blizzard
description: A blizzard is defined by wind (35 mph or more), visibility (under a quarter mile in falling or blowing snow) and duration (3 hours or more), not by how much snow falls.

facts.text: The NWS defines a blizzard as sustained wind or frequent gusts of 35 mph or more with considerable falling and/or blowing snow frequently reducing visibility to less than a quarter mile, for 3 hours or longer; when blowing snow alone causes it, it is a ground blizzard.

title: How lake-effect snow forms
description: Cold air crossing the warmer, unfrozen Great Lakes gains heat and moisture, rises and dumps narrow bands of heavy snow on downwind shores.

facts.text: Lake-effect snow forms when cold air, often from Canada, crosses the unfrozen, relatively warm Great Lakes in late fall and winter; warmth and moisture pass into the lowest air, which becomes less dense than the cold air above and rises, forming clouds and snow on the leeward shores.

Lake-effect snow falls in narrow bands that can drop 2 to 3 inches an hour or more; the sun may shine a mile or two away, skies can turn to blinding snow in minutes, totals vary from a trace to several inches over short distances, and wind shifts move the bands.

title: What feeds and stops lake-effect snow
description: A longer path over open water and a bigger lake-air temperature difference add moisture; the snow slows when the lakes freeze over.

facts.text: The more lake the wind crosses and the bigger the temperature difference, the more water the air takes in; it usually falls within about 25 miles, sometimes 100; lake-effect snow slows around February, when the lakes freeze and the air can no longer take their moisture.

title: Hurricanes can spawn tornadoes
description: Landfalling hurricanes often, but not always, produce tornadoes; some make none and others cause major outbreaks.

facts.text: Landfalling hurricanes often, but not always, spawn tornadoes: some produce none while others cause major outbreaks; Hurricane Andrew (1992) made none across South Florida but several across the Deep South after crossing the Gulf.

title: Seasonal lag
description: The hottest weeks come well after the longest day because daytime heating keeps outpacing nighttime cooling for weeks; winter's coldest weather lags the same way.

facts.text: Solar radiation reaching the Northern Hemisphere peaks at the summer solstice on June 21, but temperatures keep rising for several weeks because daytime heating from the sun stays greater than nighttime cooling.
On average, most locations in the contiguous United States have their hottest day of the year between July 15 and 31.
The warmest part of summer lags the summer solstice, just as the warmest part of the day usually comes several hours after noon, because ground and water take time to heat up.
Winter lags too: in the UK the coldest weather usually comes in January or February, well after the winter solstice in December.

title: Water's slow warming
description: Water covers most of Earth and needs far more heat, and more time, to warm than land does, which is the main reason summer peaks late, especially near cold coasts.

facts.text: The main reason for seasonal lag is that water, which covers over 70% of Earth's surface, has a much higher heat capacity than land: it takes more heat, and longer, to warm up.
In San Francisco, where a persistent marine layer of low clouds over chilly coastal water keeps early summer cool, normal daily highs peak on October 2.

title: Köppen's first letter
description: Köppen's first letter sorts climates by temperature thresholds (A tropical: coolest month 18 °C or more; E polar: warmest month below 10 °C), except B, which is set by dryness.

facts.text: In Köppen's system, tropical A climates have a coolest month of 18 °C or more, polar E climates have a warmest month below 10 °C, C and D are midlatitude climates set by temperature, and dry B climates are set by dryness.

title: Reading a Köppen code
description: Later letters add rainfall and heat: f no dry season, s dry summer, w dry winter; W desert and S steppe; h hot and k cold. Cs is the Mediterranean climate.

facts.text: Köppen's second letter describes rainfall (f: no dry season, s: dry summer, w: dry winter); in dry B climates W means desert and S semiarid steppe, and h or k marks hot or cold.
The Mediterranean climate, Köppen's Cs, has hot, dry summers and cool, wet winters; it lies between about 30° and 45° latitude on the western sides of continents, including southern California.

title: Fast carbon cycle: carbon in
description: Over a lifespan, plants and phytoplankton pull carbon dioxide from the air and build it into sugar using sunlight.

facts.text: In the fast carbon cycle, carbon moves between the atmosphere and living things on the timescale of a lifespan.
Plants and phytoplankton are the main parts of the fast carbon cycle: using energy from the Sun, they combine carbon dioxide and water to form sugar and oxygen.

title: Fast carbon cycle: carbon out
description: Carbon goes back to the air as plants and animals burn sugar for energy, as bacteria decay dead matter, and in fires.

facts.text: Carbon returns to the air as plants break down sugar for energy, animals eat plants or plankton and do the same, dead plants and plankton decay as bacteria eat them, or fire burns them; the carbon dioxide usually ends up in the atmosphere.

title: Weathering stores carbon in stone
description: Carbonic acid rain dissolves rock; the dissolved minerals reach the sea, where shell builders turn them into calcium carbonate that becomes limestone.

facts.text: In the slow carbon cycle, carbon dioxide combines with rainwater to form a weak acid, carbonic acid, that dissolves rock (chemical weathering), and the dissolved minerals flow to the ocean.

In the ocean, shell builders such as corals and plankton turn the calcium into calcium carbonate; after they die their shells settle and are cemented into limestone, locking carbon away for millions of years.

title: Earth's slow carbon thermostat
description: Most carbon sits in rock. Volcanoes return it as carbon dioxide, and because weathering speeds up when it's warm, the cycle keeps climate in check over millions of years.

facts.text: Most of Earth's carbon is stored in rocks; the rest is in the ocean, atmosphere, plants, soil and fossil fuels.
The slow carbon cycle returns carbon to the air through volcanoes: carbon-bearing rock carried deep into the Earth melts, and its carbon is released as carbon dioxide.

Weathering speeds up when it is warmer: if volcanoes raise carbon dioxide, temperatures rise, more rain dissolves more rock and more carbon ends up on the ocean floor, so the balance acts like a thermostat.

title: Snowball Earth
description: About 720 to 635 million years ago ice may have reached the Equator; volcanic carbon dioxide ended it, leaving cap carbonates on the glacial deposits.

facts.text: During the Cryogenian Period, about 720 to 635 million years ago (named from the Greek for frost or ice), much if not all of Earth's surface was covered in ice.
The Snowball Earth hypothesis proposes that ice covered land and oceans from the poles to the Equator; magnetic evidence in ancient rocks shows ice-laid deposits formed near the Equator.
The Snowball Earth hypothesis is still debated; some scientists favor a 'Slushball Earth' that kept some open water.
Volcanoes kept releasing carbon dioxide while weathering and photosynthesis, its main sinks, were suppressed on the frozen planet, so it built up until its greenhouse warming melted the ice.
Layered limestone or dolomite rocks called cap carbonates sit directly on top of Snowball Earth glacial deposits and are found at over 50 places, including Death Valley, Namibia and Australia.

title: Hothouse Earth
description: About 56 million years ago the poles had no ice caps and palms grew above the Arctic Circle; across 485 million years, carbon dioxide has been the main control on temperature.

facts.text: About 56 million years ago, during much of the Paleocene and early Eocene, the poles were free of ice caps and palm trees lived above the Arctic Circle.
A 2024 study reconstructing 485 million years of global temperature concluded, in Jessica Tierney's words, that 'carbon dioxide is the dominant control on global temperatures across geological time.'

title: How ice cores trap old air
description: Buried snow is squeezed into firn and ice, sealing air bubbles and leaving yearly layers; Antarctic cores reach back 800,000 years.

facts.text: Ice cores, mostly from Antarctica and Greenland, reach about 3 km deep; the oldest continuous records go back 123,000 years in Greenland and 800,000 years in Antarctica.
As snow piles up it is compressed into denser firn and then ice, and air is sealed into bubbles that hold a sample of the atmosphere of the time.
Seasonal differences in the snow leave annual layers in ice cores, like rings in trees, though they become harder to see deeper down.

title: What ice cores show
description: Bubbles give carbon dioxide directly and water isotopes give temperature; over 800,000 years both rose and fell together through glacial cycles about 100,000 years apart.

facts.text: Air bubbles in ice cores give past concentrations of gases such as carbon dioxide and methane directly, while ratios of water isotopes in the ice record past temperature.

The 800,000-year EPICA Dome C core shows long, cold glacial periods broken roughly every 100,000 years by warm interglacials, the latest being the last 11,000 years, with carbon dioxide low in cold times and high in warm ones.

title: Three orbital cycles
description: Earth's orbit shape (about 100,000 years), tilt (about 41,000 years) and wobble (about 26,000 years) slowly shift where and when sunlight falls.

facts.text: Earth's orbit and axis change in three cycles: the orbit's shape (eccentricity) over about 100,000 years, the tilt (obliquity) between 22.1° and 24.5° over about 41,000 years, and a top-like wobble (precession) over about 26,000 years.

title: Orbits pace the ice ages
description: Milankovitch argued cool northern summers let ice sheets grow; in 1976 foraminifera shells in deep-sea cores showed climate swings matching the orbital cycles.

facts.text: Serbian scientist Milutin Milankovitch, born in 1879, reasoned that cooler summers at high northern latitudes reduce snowmelt, letting snow build up year after year into ice sheets.
As ice cover grows it reflects more of the Sun's energy back into space, promoting further cooling.

In 1976, the study 'Variations in the Earth's Orbit: Pacemaker of the Ice Ages' used deep-sea sediment cores to show that major climate changes over the past 450,000 years matched changes in Earth's orbit.
Oxygen isotope ratios in the shells of foraminifera from deep-sea cores were instrumental in discovering the orbital theory of the ice ages.
Foraminiferans are single-celled organisms found in almost all marine waters; their shells sink when they die, and limestone and chalk are products of such seafloor deposits.
Ice ages came about every 41,000 years between one and three million years ago; about 800,000 years ago the cycle lengthened to 100,000 years, and scientists do not yet have a clear explanation.

title: The Last Glacial Maximum
description: About 20,000 years ago Earth was about 6 °C colder, ice covered North America to Wisconsin, and the world was dry, dusty and low in carbon dioxide.

facts.text: At the Last Glacial Maximum, about 20,000 years ago, Earth's average temperature was about 46 °F (8 °C), roughly 6 °C colder than today; Jessica Tierney called that 'a huge change.'
At the Last Glacial Maximum the Laurentide, Cordilleran and Greenland ice sheets covered North America, reaching as far south as Wisconsin.
The Last Glacial Maximum was generally arid, with less moisture and plant cover, expanded deserts and dusty air, and carbon dioxide as low as about 180 parts per million.

title: Loess: ice-age dust
description: Ice sheets ground rock to silt that winds spread as loess, which covers about 10% of land and makes fertile soils along the Mississippi and Missouri.

facts.text: Loess is windblown silt; ice sheets ground rock into fine particles that winds carried off, and loess now covers about 10% of Earth's land, including plains along the Mississippi and Missouri valleys.
Loess contains quartz, feldspars and carbonates, and the soils that form on it are typically fertile and suited to intensive farming.

title: Tambora and Pinatubo
description: Tambora's 1815 eruption led to the 1816 'year without a summer'; Pinatubo's 1991 haze circled the globe in weeks and cooled Earth about 0.5 °C.

facts.text: Mount Tambora in Indonesia erupted in April 1815, the largest and most destructive volcanic event in recorded history.
In 1816, western Europe and eastern North America had sporadic heavy snow and killing frost through June, July and August, crops failed, and it became known as the 'year without a summer.'
The June 1991 eruption of Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines put a sulfate aerosol cloud in the stratosphere that spread around the globe in about 3 weeks and covered it within about a year.
Pinatubo's aerosols cooled Earth's surface by an estimated 0.5 °C in 1992.

title: Sulfur, not size
description: An eruption cools the climate through sulfur dioxide lofted into the stratosphere, not through ash, and the sulfur released doesn't always scale with the eruption's size.

facts.text: The volume of magma a volcano erupts and the amount of sulfur dioxide it releases are not always proportional.

The most significant climate impacts of eruptions come from sulfur dioxide injected into the stratosphere, where it becomes sulfuric acid aerosols that reflect sunlight; injected ash falls out within days to weeks.

title: Pacemaker and amplifier
description: Orbital cycles set the timing of the ice ages, while carbon dioxide and retreating or growing ice amplify the small changes they cause.

facts.text: Warmings out of glacial periods are thought to be paced by changes in Earth's orbit, but the small changes these cause are amplified, mainly by rising carbon dioxide and by retreating ice reflecting less sunlight.
Through most of the roughly 6,000-year warming out of the last glacial period, Antarctic temperature and carbon dioxide rose together.

title: The Keeling Curve climbs
description: Carbon dioxide measured at Mauna Loa since 1958 has risen every year, from about 315 ppm to about 425 ppm in 2024, because natural sinks absorb only about half of human emissions.

facts.text: C. David Keeling of the Scripps Institution of Oceanography started measuring carbon dioxide at Mauna Loa Observatory, Hawaii, in March 1958; it is the longest record of direct CO2 measurements in the atmosphere.
Atmospheric carbon dioxide was already about 315 ppm when Mauna Loa observations began in 1958; the Mauna Loa annual average in 2024 was about 425 ppm (424.61 ppm).
Before the Industrial Revolution, atmospheric carbon dioxide was 280 ppm or less; it is now about 50 percent higher.
Natural sinks, including plant growth and ocean absorption, remove about half of the carbon dioxide humans emit from fossil fuels; the rest stays in the atmosphere, so the total rises each year.

title: The Keeling Curve's yearly zigzag
description: Carbon dioxide falls each northern spring and summer as plants grow and rises each autumn and winter as they decay; the Southern Hemisphere has a weaker, opposite cycle.

facts.text: The yearly CO2 cycle comes from plants: in Northern Hemisphere spring and summer they draw in CO2 to grow; in autumn and winter growth slows and decay releases it. At Mauna Loa the highest monthly value comes each May.

The Southern Hemisphere shows a similar but less intense CO2 cycle in opposite seasons; because the Northern Hemisphere has much more land and vegetation, the global yearly cycle follows the northern seasons.

title: Carbon fingerprints of fossil fuels
description: Fossil fuels carry plants' low carbon-13 and no carbon-14, so their carbon shows up as a falling carbon-13 share in the air: the extra carbon is ours.

facts.text: Plants hold less carbon-13 than the air, and coal and oil, the remains of ancient plants and animals, share that low-carbon-13 fingerprint; the air's share of carbon-13 is steadily decreasing because of fossil fuel emissions.
Fossil fuels contain no carbon-14, the heaviest form of carbon, and changes in the air's carbon-14 show that the rise in carbon dioxide is dominated by fossil fuel emissions.
Fossil fuels like coal and oil hold carbon from millions of years of photosynthesis; burning them returns that carbon to the atmosphere in just a few hundred years.

title: Oxygen and volcano clues
description: The air's oxygen is slowly falling as fossil fuels burn, and humans emit many times more carbon dioxide than all volcanoes, ruling volcanoes out as the source.

facts.text: Atmospheric oxygen levels are decreasing globally, mainly because of fossil-fuel burning; the changes are far too small to affect human health.
Human activities emit 60 or more times as much carbon dioxide each year as all the world's volcanoes.

title: Building the temperature record
description: The global record joins land weather stations with ship, buoy and satellite sea temperatures, converts readings to anomalies, and is checked by independent groups.

facts.text: Land weather stations cover only about a third of the planet, so the global temperature record adds sea surface temperatures from ships, buoys and, more recently, satellites.
To track change, scientists convert temperature readings into anomalies: the difference between the observed temperature and the long-term average for that location and date.
Multiple independent research groups around the world analyze the surface temperature data themselves, and they all show a similar upward trend.

title: About 1.1 °C of warming
description: Earth's surface was about 1.1 °C warmer in 2011 to 2020 than in 1850 to 1900, land more than ocean, and each of the last four decades beat every decade before it.

facts.text: IPCC AR6: global surface temperature was about 1.1 °C (1.09 °C) higher in 2011 to 2020 than in 1850 to 1900, with larger increases over land than over the ocean.
Each of the last four decades has been successively warmer than any decade that preceded it since 1850.

title: Why the Sun is cleared
description: Satellites show no upward trend in the Sun's energy since 1978, and the stratosphere is cooling while the surface warms, the pattern of heat-trapping gases rather than a brighter Sun.

facts.text: Since 1978, satellite sensors tracking the Sun's energy reaching the top of the atmosphere have shown no upward trend.
If the Sun were driving global warming, all layers of the atmosphere would warm; instead the surface is warming and the stratosphere is cooling, consistent with heat-trapping gases.

title: Natural drivers add almost nothing
description: The IPCC finds the Sun and volcanoes together changed global temperature by only about -0.1 to +0.1 °C since 1850 to 1900, while human causes likely added 0.8 to 1.3 °C.

facts.text: IPCC AR6: human activities likely caused 0.8 to 1.3 °C of warming from 1850 to 1900 to 2010 to 2019 (best estimate 1.07 °C), while natural drivers, the Sun and volcanoes, changed it by only -0.1 to +0.1 °C.

title: Positive and negative feedbacks
description: A feedback is a loop in which a change sets off effects that amplify it (positive) or reduce it (negative).

facts.text: A climate feedback is a process that amplifies or reduces a change over time, such as water vapor increasing as Earth warms and causing even more warming.

title: The snow and ice feedback
description: Snow reflects most sunlight; when warming melts it, darker ground absorbs more, which warms and melts further: a positive feedback.

facts.text: Snow reflects 80 to 90 percent of incoming sunlight, while trees, plants and soil reflect only 10 to 30 percent.
With less snow cover, the land reflects less energy to space and absorbs more sunlight, which melts more snow: a positive feedback. Like black clothes, darker surfaces absorb more solar energy.

title: The water vapor feedback
description: Warmer air holds about 7% more water vapor per 1 °C; the extra vapor traps more heat, more than doubling CO2's warming, but vapor follows temperature rather than driving it.

facts.text: For every 1 °C the atmosphere warms, the amount of water vapor it holds can increase by about 7 percent.

Water vapor is Earth's most abundant greenhouse gas but a consequence of warming, not its cause: extra vapor amplifies warming, by more than double CO2's effect alone, and a molecule stays aloft only about nine days.

title: Climate sensitivity: about 3 °C
description: Equilibrium climate sensitivity, the eventual warming from doubled CO2, is best estimated at 3 °C, likely 2.5 to 4 °C and very likely 2 to 5 °C (IPCC AR6).

facts.text: Equilibrium climate sensitivity (ECS) is, by definition, the eventual global warming after the carbon dioxide in the atmosphere doubles and the climate has adjusted.
IPCC AR6 (2021): the best estimate of equilibrium climate sensitivity is 3 °C, with a likely range of 2.5 to 4 °C and a very likely range of 2 to 5 °C, narrower than AR5's likely 1.5 to 4.5 °C.

The IPCC's ECS range combines multiple lines of evidence: understanding of climate processes, the instrumental record, past climates and model-based constraints; in its terms "likely" means a 66 to 100% chance.

title: Clouds keep it a range
description: Clouds are the largest remaining uncertainty in climate feedbacks, which is why sensitivity is a range, though a cloud feedback that dampens warming is now very unlikely.

facts.text: Clouds remain the largest part of the uncertainty in climate feedbacks, but IPCC AR6 judges a cloud feedback that dampens future warming to be very unlikely.

title: Greenland and Antarctica losing ice
description: GRACE satellites show both ice sheets losing mass since 2002, through surface melting and outlet glaciers where warming ocean water plays a key role.

facts.text: The GRACE (Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment) and GRACE Follow-On satellites show both ice sheets losing mass since 2002: Greenland roughly 260 billion tons a year and Antarctica roughly 135 billion (2002 to 2025).
Ice-sheet mass loss is greatest where ice flows into large outlet glaciers, and warming ocean water near the ice sheets plays a key role in the losses.

IPCC AR6: human influence has very likely contributed to the surface melting of the Greenland Ice Sheet over the past two decades, but there is only limited evidence of human influence on Antarctic ice loss.

title: Ice sheets respond for centuries
description: Glaciers and ice sheets are committed to keep melting for decades or centuries; Greenland will virtually certainly and Antarctica likely keep losing ice this century, at a pace that is deeply uncertain.

facts.text: IPCC AR6: mountain and polar glaciers are committed to continue melting for decades or centuries; continued ice loss over the 21st century is virtually certain for Greenland and likely for Antarctica.

IPCC AR6: ice-sheet instabilities, in some cases involving tipping points, are low-likelihood, high-impact outcomes with deep uncertainty that could strongly increase Antarctic ice loss for centuries under high emissions.

title: Emissions by sector
description: In 2019 energy supply made about 34% of human greenhouse gas emissions, industry 24%, farming, forestry and land use 22%, transport 15% and buildings 6%.

facts.text: IPCC AR6: in 2019, about 34% of global net human greenhouse gas emissions came from energy supply, 24% from industry, 22% from agriculture, forestry and other land use, 15% from transport and 6% from buildings.
Burning coal, natural gas and oil for electricity and heat is the largest single source of global greenhouse gas emissions.

title: Where each gas comes from
description: CO2 comes mainly from fossil fuels and also from clearing forests and making cement; methane from farming, waste and energy; nitrous oxide mainly from farming such as fertilizer use.

facts.text: Fossil fuel use is the main source of CO2, which also comes from deforestation and land clearing; methane comes from agriculture, waste, energy and biomass burning; nitrous oxide mainly from agriculture, such as fertilizer use.
Making cement releases CO2 two ways: heating limestone decomposes its calcium carbonate into lime and CO2, and the fossil fuels burned to heat the raw materials add more.

title: Warming loads the weather dice
description: Hot extremes and heavy downpours have become more frequent and intense since the 1950s, driven mainly by human warming; the link to tornadoes is still uncertain.

facts.text: IPCC AR6: it is virtually certain that hot extremes, including heatwaves, have become more frequent and more intense across most land regions since the 1950s, with human-induced climate change the main driver.
IPCC AR6: heavy precipitation events have become more frequent and intense since the 1950s over most land areas with enough data, and human-induced climate change is likely the main driver.
Scientists have low confidence in any link between climate change and tornado activity so far, partly because tornadoes are small and short-lived, which makes them very difficult to model.

title: Testing a single event
description: Attribution studies compare models of today's climate with a climate without human influence to measure how much more likely or intense an event has become.

facts.text: An attribution study compares computer simulations of today's climate with simulations that remove the human influence, to see how much more likely or intense a weather event has become.
World Weather Attribution found climate change made the record July 2019 heatwave in France and the Netherlands at least 10 times more likely (about 100 times by its central estimate).

title: Unequivocal: human influence has warmed Earth
description: The IPCC concludes it is unequivocal that human influence has warmed the atmosphere, ocean and land, and that the rise in greenhouse gases since about 1750 is caused by human activities.

facts.text: IPCC AR6: it is unequivocal that human influence has warmed the atmosphere, ocean and land, and increases in well-mixed greenhouse gases since around 1750 are unequivocally caused by human activities.

title: Observing the atmosphere
description: Forecasts start from observations: radiosondes on weather balloons sample the air as they climb, Doppler radar finds precipitation and its motion, and geostationary satellites watch whole regions without a break.

facts.text: A radiosonde carried up by a weather balloon radios back pressure, temperature, relative humidity and GPS position every second, its tracked position gives the winds, and it can climb higher than 35 km (about 115,000 feet).
The National Weather Service launches radiosondes from 92 stations, and more than 800 upper-air stations around the world launch at the same times each day, near 00:00 and 12:00 UTC.

A WSR-88D weather radar sends out pulses of energy that scatter off raindrops, snow, hail, bugs or dust; it transmits for only about 7 seconds each hour and spends the rest of the time listening for echoes.

The radar's computers measure each returned pulse's strength, travel time and Doppler (phase) shift, the same effect that changes a passing train whistle's pitch, which shows whether the target is moving toward or away from the radar.
NOAA's GOES weather satellites orbit 22,236 miles above the Equator at a speed matching Earth's rotation, so each stays over the same region and watches it continuously.

title: How a weather model forecasts
description: A weather model gathers observations into a picture of the atmosphere now, solves the equations of physics at many points and levels, and steps forward in time, over and over.

facts.text: Weather models ingest observations from satellites, aircraft, balloons and even personal weather stations, solve physics equations for temperature, dew point, wind and more at many levels, and feed each time step's result back in, repeating to reach days ahead.

title: What a chance of rain means
description: A National Weather Service chance of rain is the probability of at least 0.01 inch at a given point during the forecast period, not the share of the day or the area that gets wet.

facts.text: In a National Weather Service forecast, the probability of precipitation is the chance that at least 0.01 inch of rain falls at a given point during the forecast period; a 40 percent chance means a 40 percent probability of that at the point, not rain over 40 percent of the time or area.

title: Why forecast skill fades
description: Forecasts lose accuracy with range because the atmosphere is chaotic: small errors in the starting picture grow. Forecasters run ensembles from slightly different starts and turn their spread into probabilities.

facts.text: According to NOAA, a five-day forecast is accurate about 90 percent of the time and a seven-day forecast about 80 percent, but a forecast of 10 days or more is right only about half the time, because longer ranges rely more on estimates and assumptions.

The atmosphere is a chaotic system: because observations are limited and unevenly spread, the estimate of its current state always has small errors, and those errors grow until they have a major impact on the forecast.
Forecast centers run their model many times from slightly different starting conditions, an ensemble, and use the spread of outcomes to compute probabilities of possible weather.

title: Forecasting beyond two weeks
description: Day-by-day weather forecasts run out at around two weeks. Beyond that, outlooks draw on slow parts of the Earth system, such as ocean heat, sea ice, snowpack and soil moisture, that keep a memory of their state.

facts.text: NOAA describes a gap between traditional weather forecasts and longer climate outlooks, the subseasonal-to-seasonal timescale, running from about two weeks ahead to months ahead.

For forecasts weeks to months ahead, predictability comes from parts of the Earth system that change more slowly than weather, such as upper-ocean heat, sea ice, snowpack and soil moisture, which keep a memory of their earlier state.

title: Watch versus warning
description: A watch means conditions favor a hazard, so get ready; a warning means it is happening or about to, so act. Warnings cover much smaller areas than watches.

facts.text: An NWS tornado watch means tornadoes are possible in and near the watch area, which typically covers numerous counties or even states; people should review emergency plans, check supplies and their safe room, and be ready to act quickly.
A flood watch is issued when conditions are favorable for flooding; it does not mean flooding will occur, but it is possible.

An NWS tornado warning means a tornado has been sighted or indicated by weather radar and there is imminent danger to life and property; a warning covers a much smaller area than a watch, around the size of a city or small county.
A flash flood warning is issued when a flash flood is imminent or occurring, and people in flood-prone areas should move immediately to high ground.

title: What to do when a warning comes
description: In a tornado warning, go to an interior room on the lowest floor of a sturdy building, away from windows. In a flash flood warning, get to high ground. Hurricane watches and warnings come 48 and 36 hours ahead of tropical-storm-force winds.

facts.text: In a tornado warning, the NWS says to move to an interior room on the lowest floor of a sturdy building and avoid windows; people in a mobile home, a vehicle or outdoors should move to the closest substantial shelter.

The National Hurricane Center issues a hurricane watch 48 hours before it expects tropical-storm-force winds and a hurricane warning 36 hours before, when preparations should be complete; people should evacuate immediately if ordered.

title: Volcano alert levels
description: The USGS rates volcanoes Normal, Advisory, Watch or Warning. Warning means a hazardous eruption is imminent, underway or suspected.

facts.text: USGS volcano alert levels run Normal, Advisory, Watch and Warning; Watch means heightened unrest with an increased chance of eruption, and Warning means a hazardous eruption is imminent, underway or suspected.

title: Earthquakes: forecast, not predicted
description: A true prediction needs date and time, place and magnitude, and no scientist has ever predicted a major quake. Scientists give probabilities instead, and there is no such thing as earthquake weather.

facts.text: A true earthquake prediction must give the date and time, the location and the magnitude; neither the USGS nor any other scientists have ever predicted a major earthquake, and they do not expect to know how in the foreseeable future.
Instead of predicting, USGS scientists calculate the probability that a significant earthquake will occur in a specific area within a certain number of years.

There is no such thing as earthquake weather: earthquakes happen about equally in cold, hot and rainy weather, and most occur several kilometers below the surface, deeper than rainwater can easily reach.

title: Drop, Cover and Hold On
description: In an earthquake, drop to hands and knees, cover head and neck under something sturdy, and hold on until the shaking stops. Falling and flying objects cause most injuries; doorways and running outside don't help.

facts.text: Drop, Cover and Hold On: drop onto hands and knees before the shaking knocks you down, cover head and neck (under a sturdy table or desk if near), hold on until the shaking stops, ready to move with your shelter; in bed, turn face down under a pillow.

Most earthquake injuries and deaths come from falling or flying objects (TVs, lamps, glass, bookcases) or being knocked down; doorways don't protect against falling objects, and staying put is safer than running outside or to other rooms.

title: Why heat is dangerous
description: Extreme heat is the top weather-related killer in the US. The body cools by evaporating sweat, and humid air slows that down, which is what the heat index measures.

facts.text: The National Weather Service calls extreme heat the number one weather-related killer in the United States.

The body cools itself by sweating, and evaporating sweat carries heat away; when humidity is high, sweat evaporates more slowly and the body struggles to cool, which is why the heat index, what the temperature feels like, rises with humidity.

title: Heat illness and who is at risk
description: Heat exhaustion brings heavy sweating and cold, clammy skin; heat stroke brings a body temperature of 103°F or more, hot skin and confusion, and is a 911 emergency. Children, older adults, people with chronic illnesses and pregnant women are most vulnerable.

facts.text: CDC warning signs: heat exhaustion brings heavy sweating, cold, pale and clammy skin and a fast, weak pulse; heat stroke brings a body temperature of 103°F or higher, hot, red, dry or damp skin, a fast, strong pulse and confusion.
The CDC says heat stroke is a medical emergency, so call 911 right away; for heat exhaustion, move to a cool place, loosen clothes, use cool, wet cloths and sip water.

The NWS lists infants and children, older adults (especially those with health conditions or living alone), people with chronic medical conditions and pregnant women as particularly vulnerable to heat, and advises checking on older, sick or frail people.

title: Urban heat islands
description: Roofs and roads soak up and re-emit heat and cities have fewer trees, so US cities run about 1 to 7°F warmer by day and 2 to 5°F warmer at night than outlying areas.

facts.text: Buildings and roads absorb and re-emit more of the Sun's heat than forests and water, cities have fewer trees for shade and transpiration, and in the US urban areas run about 1 to 7°F warmer by day and 2 to 5°F warmer at night than outlying areas.

title: How flash floods form
description: A flash flood begins within hours of heavy rain. It comes fastest where rain can't soak in, such as on saturated soil or pavement, and it can strike downstream of the rain.

facts.text: A flash flood is flooding that begins within 6 hours, and often within 3 hours, of heavy rainfall, most often from thunderstorms; how fast it comes depends on rainfall intensity, land use, slope, vegetation, soil type and how much water the soil already holds.
Flash flooding is possible anywhere: normally quiet creeks can become raging torrents when heavy rain falls overhead or even upstream, and city streets and highway underpasses can flood.

In forests much of the rain soaks into the soil and reaches streams slowly; in cities, roofs, roads and parking lots stop it soaking in, so more water reaches streams more quickly, making floods more frequent and more severe.

title: Turn Around, Don't Drown
description: Six inches of fast water can knock over an adult and a foot can carry away most cars. Most flood drownings happen in vehicles, so never drive or walk into floodwater.

facts.text: The NWS says 6 inches of fast-moving floodwater can knock over an adult, 12 inches of rushing water can carry away most cars and 2 feet can carry away SUVs and trucks.
Over half of flood-related drownings occur when a vehicle is driven into hazardous floodwater, and the road beneath the water may have collapsed.
The NWS and Ready.gov rule is Turn Around, Don't Drown: never drive around barriers on a flooded road, and never drive or walk into floodwater, however passable it looks.

title: What drives a wildfire
description: Fire needs heat, oxygen and fuel. A wildfire's behavior depends on fuels, weather and topography: dry fuel, wind, low humidity and slopes speed it up.

facts.text: Fire needs heat, oxygen and fuel (the fire triangle), and how a wildfire behaves depends on a second triangle of fuels, weather and topography.
Moisture is the most important trait of wildland fuel: live trees usually hold a great deal of moisture and dead logs very little, and a fire's heat must drive off moisture before fuel burns.

Wind brings a fresh supply of oxygen and pushes fire toward new fuel; at low humidity fuels dry out, catch fire more easily and burn faster; and a wildfire typically moves more quickly uphill than downhill or on flat ground.

title: Longer fire seasons
description: Fire seasons in parts of the western US are more than a month longer than 35 years ago. NASA points to warming (hotter weather, earlier snowmelt, less summer rain) together with fuel built up by decades of fire suppression.

facts.text: Looking back over 35 years of weather data, U.S. Forest Service scientists found fire seasons starting earlier in spring and running later into autumn; parts of the western United States now have fire seasons more than a month longer than 35 years ago.

NASA says hotter weather, earlier snowmelt, warmer nights and less summer rain are increasing fire activity, while decades of fire suppression built up fuel in some forests; together they raise the potential for extreme fires.

title: The Paris Agreement's goals
description: Reached at COP21 in December 2015, the Paris Agreement aims to hold warming well below 2°C and pursue 1.5°C, with each country setting its own plan every five years.

facts.text: The Paris Agreement was reached at the COP21 climate conference in Paris on 12 December 2015 and entered into force on 4 November 2016.

The Paris Agreement's long-term goal is to hold the rise in global temperature to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C; it also aims to strengthen abilities to adapt to climate impacts and to provide finance to developing countries.

Under the Paris Agreement, every five years each country is expected to submit an updated national climate action plan, a nationally determined contribution, setting out the actions it will take to cut emissions.

title: Mitigation and adaptation
description: Mitigation cuts the flow of greenhouse gases or strengthens carbon sinks; adaptation adjusts to the climate we have or expect, to lower risks like rising seas and extreme weather.

facts.text: NASA describes mitigation, reducing greenhouse gas flows by cutting sources such as fossil fuel burning or enhancing sinks such as oceans, forests and soil, and adaptation, adjusting to actual or expected climate to reduce risks like sea-level rise and extreme weather.

title: Weighing climate policy options
description: Each option for cutting emissions has supporters and critics. Carbon pricing is called cost-effective but can weigh more on lower-income households; nuclear power emits no CO2 while running but leaves long-lived radioactive waste.

facts.text: C2ES describes carbon pricing as a cost-effective way to cut emissions, but notes that lower-income households spend a larger share of income on energy, so higher energy costs can hit them harder, and that directing revenue to those households can offset the costs.
Nuclear reactors produce no carbon dioxide or air pollution while operating, but nuclear power creates radioactive waste that can remain dangerous to human health for thousands of years.

title: Solar geoengineering research
description: Stratospheric aerosol injection would copy the cooling of big volcanic eruptions. It might cool quickly but does nothing about greenhouse gases and has poorly understood side effects; a 2021 National Academies report backed research only.

facts.text: Stratospheric aerosol injection, a proposed solar geoengineering method, would mimic the temporary cooling of some big eruptions; GAO notes it might cool quickly but doesn't address greenhouse gas buildup and has poorly understood effects on rainfall and ozone.

A 2021 National Academies report recommended that the United States develop a research program on solar geoengineering, while saying that cutting emissions and adapting to climate impacts are the first line of defense.

title: Myth: the ozone hole causes warming
description: The ozone hole lets in extra ultraviolet light, which can't explain surface warming; its role in global warming is small compared with other human impacts.

facts.text: Extra ultraviolet light reaching the surface through the ozone hole cannot explain the warming of Earth's surface, and NASA says the ozone hole's role in global warming is small compared with the impacts of other human activities.

title: Myth: a cold snap disproves warming
description: Climate is a long-term average and weather changes by the hour. Earth has warmed, yet blizzards and freezes still happen each winter, just likely less often.

facts.text: Earth has been getting warmer over the past 100 years or so, but that doesn't mean it never gets cold: blizzards, snowstorms and freezing temperatures can still happen each winter, though cold days are likely to become less frequent.
Climate is described by long-term averages of weather, often over 30 years (Climate Normals), while weather can change in minutes or hours.

title: Myth: volcanoes out-emit people
description: Human activities emit 60 or more times as much CO2 each year as all volcanoes, and today's eruptions have never caused detectable warming; their sulfur tends to cool.

facts.text: Human activities emit 60 or more times as much carbon dioxide each year as all the world's volcanoes.
Carbon dioxide from present-day volcanic eruptions has never caused detectable global warming, while their sulfur dioxide has occasionally caused detectable global cooling.
